## 1. Chapter on Awakening
## 1. Awakening Sutta
1. Thus have I heard—At one time the Blessed One was staying at Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's monastery. There the Blessed One addressed the monks: 

"Monks, if wanderers of other sects should ask you: 'Friends, what is the supporting condition for the development of the things that lead to awakening?' Being thus asked, monks, how would you answer those wanderers of other sects?"

"Venerable Sir, our teachings are rooted in the Blessed One, [guided by the Blessed One, and have the Blessed One as their resort. It would be good if the Blessed One himself would clarify the meaning of this statement. Having heard it from the Blessed One, the monks will remember it.]"

"Then listen, monks, and pay close attention; I will speak." "Yes, Venerable Sir," those monks replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:

"Monks, if wanderers of other sects should ask you: 'Friends, what is the supporting condition for the development of the things that lead to awakening?' Being thus
164:
asked, monks, you should answer those wanderers of other sects in this way:

'Here, friends, a monk has good friends, good companions, and good associates. Friends, this is the first supporting condition for the development of the things that lead to awakening.'

'Furthermore, friends, a monk is virtuous; he dwells restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha, endowed with proper conduct and resort; seeing danger in the slightest faults, he trains himself by undertaking the rules of training. Friends, this is the second supporting condition for the development of the things that lead to awakening.'

'Furthermore, friends, a monk obtains at will, without difficulty or trouble, talk that is conducive to effacement and suitable for opening up the heart—that is, talk on wanting little, talk on contentment, talk on seclusion, talk on non-entanglement, talk on arousing energy, talk on virtue, talk on concentration, talk on wisdom, talk on liberation, and talk on the knowledge and vision of liberation. Friends, this is the third supporting condition for the development of the things that lead to awakening.'

'Furthermore, friends, a monk dwells with energy aroused for abandoning unwholesome states and acquiring wholesome states; he is steadfast, firm in effort, and does not cast off the duty regarding wholesome states. Friends, this is the fourth supporting condition for the development of the things that lead to awakening.'

'Furthermore, friends, a monk is wise; he is endowed with wisdom regarding arising and passing away, which is noble and penetrative, leading to the complete destruction of suffering. Friends, this is the fifth supporting condition for the development of the things that lead to awakening.'

"Monks, when a monk has good friends, good companions, and good associates, it is to be expected that he will be virtuous, that he will dwell restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha, endowed with proper conduct and resort, and that seeing danger in the slightest faults, he will train himself by undertaking the rules of training. Monks, when a monk has good friends, good companions, and good associates, it is to be expected that he will obtain at will, without difficulty or trouble, talk that is conducive to effacement and suitable for opening up the heart—that is, talk on wanting little,
165:
talk on contentment, talk on seclusion, talk on non-entanglement, talk on arousing energy, talk on virtue, talk on concentration, talk on wisdom, talk on liberation, and talk on the knowledge and vision of liberation.

Monks, when a monk has good friends, good companions, and good associates, it is to be expected that he will dwell with energy aroused for abandoning unwholesome states and acquiring wholesome states; he will be steadfast, firm in effort, and will not cast off the duty regarding wholesome states.

Monks, when a monk has good friends, good companions, and good associates, it is to be expected that he will be wise, endowed with wisdom regarding arising and passing away, which is noble and penetrative, leading to the complete destruction of suffering.

Furthermore, monks, when a monk is established in these five things, he should develop four additional things: the perception of the unattractive (asubha) should be developed for abandoning lust; loving-kindness (mettā) should be developed for abandoning ill will; mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānasati) should be developed for cutting off discursive thoughts; and the perception of impermanence (aniccasaññā) should be developed for the uprooting of the conceit 'I am' (asmimāna). Monks, for one who perceives impermanence, the perception of non-self (anattasaññā) becomes established. One who perceives non-self reaches the uprooting of the conceit 'I am' and attains Nibbāna in this very life."

The First Sutta.
## 2. Support Sutta
2. Then a certain monk approached the Blessed One... [and having paid homage,] sat down to one side and said to the Blessed One: "Venerable Sir, it is said, 'one possessed of support, one possessed of support.' To what extent, Venerable Sir, is a monk one possessed of support?"

"Monk, if a monk, relying on faith, abandons the unwholesome and develops the wholesome, that unwholesome is indeed abandoned by him. Monk, if a monk, relying on shame (hiri)... relying on fear of wrongdoing (ottappa)... relying on energy... relying on wisdom, abandons the unwholesome and develops the wholesome, that unwholesome is indeed abandoned by him. For that unwholesome of the monk is truly abandoned, well abandoned, when he has seen it with noble wisdom and abandoned it."
166:
Monk, that monk, having established himself in these five qualities, should dwell depending on four things. What are the four? Here, monk, a monk reflects and uses some things, reflects and endures some things, reflects and avoids some things, and reflects and removes some things. Monk, in this way, a monk is one who is accomplished in dependencies.

The Second Discourse.

## 3. Meghiya Sutta

3. On one occasion, the Blessed One was staying at Cālikā, on Cālikā Mountain. At that time, the Venerable Meghiya was the Blessed One's attendant. Then the Venerable Meghiya approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and stood to one side. Standing there, the Venerable Meghiya said to the Blessed One: "Bhante, I wish to enter Jantu village for alms."

"Meghiya, you may go when you think it is the right time."

Then, in the morning, the Venerable Meghiya dressed, took his bowl and robe, and entered Jantu village for alms. After wandering for alms in Jantu village and returning from his alms round after his meal, he approached the bank of the Kimikālā River. While walking up and down for exercise along the bank of the Kimikālā River, the Venerable Meghiya saw a mango grove that was pleasant and delightful. Upon seeing it, the thought occurred to him: "This mango grove is indeed pleasant and delightful. It is truly suitable for the striving of a clansman intent on striving. If the Blessed One would allow me, I would come to this mango grove to strive."

Then the Venerable Meghiya approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. Sitting there, the Venerable Meghiya said to the Blessed One: "Bhante, in the morning, I dressed, took my bowl and robe, and entered Jantu village for alms. After wandering for alms in Jantu village and returning from my alms round after my meal, I approached the bank of the Kimikālā River. While walking up and down for exercise along the bank of the Kimikālā River, I saw a mango grove that was pleasant and delightful. Upon seeing it, the thought occurred to me: 'This mango grove is indeed pleasant and delightful. It is truly suitable for the striving of a clansman intent on striving. If the Blessed One would allow me, I would come to this mango grove to strive.' If the Blessed One allows me, I would like to go to that mango grove to strive."

"Meghiya, I am still alone.
167:
Wait a while, Meghiya, until some other monk arrives."

A second time, the Venerable Meghiya said to the Blessed One: "Bhante, for the Blessed One, there is nothing further to be done, and no need to add to what has been done. But for me, Bhante, there is something further to be done, and a need to add to what has been done. If the Blessed One would allow me, I would like to go to that mango grove to strive."

"Wait a while, Meghiya, until some other monk arrives, as I am now alone."

A third time, the Venerable Meghiya said to the Blessed One: "Bhante, for the Blessed One, there is nothing further to be done, and no need to add to what has been done. But for me, Bhante, there is something further to be done, and a need to add to what has been done. If the Blessed One would allow me, I would like to go to that mango grove to strive."

"Meghiya, when you speak of striving, what can we say? Meghiya, you may go when you think it is the right time."

Then the Venerable Meghiya rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him on his right, approached that mango grove. Having entered the mango grove, he sat down at the foot of a certain tree for the day's abiding. While the Venerable Meghiya was staying in that mango grove, there mostly arose in him three evil, unwholesome thoughts, namely: sensual thoughts, thoughts of ill-will, and thoughts of cruelty. Then the Venerable Meghiya thought: "How wonderful! How marvelous! I have gone forth from the home life into homelessness out of faith, yet I am assailed by these three evil, unwholesome thoughts—sensual thoughts, thoughts of ill-will, and thoughts of cruelty."

Then the Venerable Meghiya approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. Sitting there, the Venerable Meghiya said to the Blessed One: "Bhante, while I was staying in that mango grove, there mostly arose in me three evil, unwholesome thoughts, namely: sensual thoughts, thoughts of ill-will, and thoughts of cruelty. Bhante, it occurred to me: 'How wonderful! How marvelous!
168:
"Venerable Sir, I have gone forth from the home life into homelessness out of faith. Yet, these three evil unwholesome thoughts constantly obsess me: thoughts of sensual desire, thoughts of ill will, and thoughts of cruelty." (Thus he spoke.)

"Meghiya, five things lead to the maturity of the liberation of mind (cetovimutti) that is not yet mature. What five? Here, Meghiya, a bhikkhu has a good friend, a good companion, a good associate. This is the first thing, Meghiya, that leads to the maturity of the liberation of mind that is not yet mature.

Furthermore, Meghiya, a bhikkhu is virtuous; he dwells restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha, possessed of proper conduct (ācāra) and resort (gocara), seeing danger in even the slightest faults, and having undertaken the training rules, he trains in them. This is the second thing, Meghiya, that leads to the maturity of the liberation of mind that is not yet mature.

Furthermore, Meghiya, there is talk that is truly sober and conducive to the opening of the mind, that is: talk on wanting little, talk on contentment, talk on seclusion, talk on non-association, talk on arousing energy, talk on virtue, talk on concentration, talk on wisdom, talk on liberation (the fruit of Arahantship), and talk on the knowledge and vision of liberation (reviewing knowledge of the fruit of Arahantship). Such talk he obtains at will, without difficulty, and without trouble. This is the third thing, Meghiya, that leads to the maturity of the liberation of mind that is not yet mature.

Furthermore, Meghiya, a bhikkhu dwells with energy aroused for the abandoning of unwholesome states and the acquisition of wholesome states; he is strong, firm in exertion, and does not neglect the duty of cultivating wholesome states. This is the fourth thing, Meghiya, that leads to the maturity of the liberation of mind that is not yet mature.

Furthermore, Meghiya, a bhikkhu is wise; he possesses wisdom that discerns the arising and passing away of things, which is noble and penetrative, leading to the complete destruction of suffering (Nibbāna). This is the fifth thing, Meghiya, that leads to the maturity of the liberation of mind that is not yet mature.

Meghiya, when a bhikkhu has a good friend, a good companion, and a good associate, it is to be expected that he will be virtuous... [and so on]."
169:
"...it is to be expected that he will undertake and train in the training rules."

"Meghiya, for a bhikkhu who has a good friend, a good companion, and a good associate, it is to be expected that he will obtain at will, without difficulty, and without trouble, such talk that is truly sober and conducive to the opening of the mind (samatha and vipassanā), that is: talk on wanting little... [as before]... and talk on the knowledge and vision of liberation."

"Meghiya, for a bhikkhu who has a good friend, a good companion, and a good associate, it is to be expected that he will dwell with energy aroused... [as before]... and will not neglect the duty of cultivating wholesome states."

"Meghiya, for a bhikkhu who has a good friend, a good companion, and a good associate, it is to be expected that he will be wise... [as before]... and will possess the noble wisdom that leads to the complete destruction of suffering, Nibbāna."

"Meghiya, when that bhikkhu is established in these five things, he should further develop four additional things: foulness (asubha) should be developed for the abandoning of lust; loving-kindness (mettā) should be developed for the abandoning of ill will; mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānasati) should be developed for the cutting off of thoughts; and the perception of impermanence (anicca-saññā) should be developed for the uprooting of the conceit 'I am' (asmimāna)."

"Meghiya, in one who perceives impermanence, the perception of non-self (anatta-saññā) becomes established. One who perceives non-self reaches the uprooting of the conceit 'I am' and attains Nibbāna in this very life." (Thus the Buddha said.)

Third Sutta.

## 4 - Nandaka Sutta

4. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's Park. At that time, the Venerable Nandaka was instructing, urging, rousing, and gladdening the bhikkhus in the assembly hall with a Dhamma talk. Then, in the evening, the Blessed One rose from his seclusion and approached the assembly hall. Having approached, he stood outside the porch waiting for the talk to end. Then, knowing that the talk had ended, the Blessed One cleared his throat and knocked on the door-bolt. Those bhikkhus opened the door for the Blessed One.
170:
Then the Blessed One entered the assembly hall and sat down on the prepared seat. Having sat down, the Blessed One said to the Venerable Nandaka: "Nandaka, this long Dhamma discourse of yours was inspired for the monks. Indeed, my back ached as I stood outside the porch waiting for the conclusion of the talk."

When this was said, the Venerable Nandaka, feeling bashful, said to the Blessed One: "Venerable Sir, we did not know that the Blessed One was standing outside the porch. Venerable Sir, if we had known that the Blessed One was standing outside the porch, we would not have spoken even this much of the Dhamma (we would not have spoken at such length)."

Then the Blessed One, knowing that the Venerable Nandaka was feeling bashful, said to him: "Good, good, Nandaka! It is fitting for you clansmen who have gone forth from the home life into homelessness out of faith to sit together for Dhamma talk. When you are gathered together, Nandaka, you should do one of two things: either Dhamma talk or noble silence.

Nandaka, a monk has faith but lacks virtue. Thus, he is incomplete in that factor. Therefore, he should fulfill that factor, thinking, 'How can I be both faithful and virtuous?' When, Nandaka, a monk is both faithful and virtuous, then he is complete in that factor.

Nandaka, a monk is faithful and virtuous, but he does not gain internal serenity of mind. Thus, he is incomplete in that factor. Therefore, he should fulfill that factor, thinking, 'How can I be faithful, virtuous, and also gain internal serenity of mind?' When, Nandaka, a monk is faithful, virtuous, and gains internal serenity of mind, then he is complete in that factor.

Nandaka, a monk is faithful, virtuous, and gains internal serenity of mind, but he does not gain insight into the nature of things through higher wisdom. Thus, he is incomplete in that factor. Nandaka, just as if there were a four-footed animal, and one of its legs was stunted and defective, it would be incomplete in its limbs; in the same way, Nandaka, a monk is faithful, virtuous, and gains internal serenity of mind, but he does not gain insight into the nature of things through higher wisdom. Thus, he is incomplete in that factor. Therefore, he should fulfill that factor, thinking, 'How can I be faithful, virtuous,
171:
gain internal serenity of mind, and also gain insight into the nature of things through higher wisdom?' When, Nandaka, a monk is faithful, virtuous, gains internal serenity of mind, and gains insight into the nature of things through higher wisdom, then he is complete in that factor."

The Blessed One said this. Having said this, the Sugata rose from his seat and entered his dwelling.

Then, soon after the Blessed One had left, the Venerable Nandaka addressed the monks: "Friends, just now the Blessed One, having proclaimed the holy life, complete in all its parts and perfectly pure, through these four factors, rose from his seat and entered his dwelling. [He said:] 'Nandaka, a monk has faith but lacks virtue. Thus, he is incomplete in that factor. Therefore, he should fulfill that factor, thinking, "How can I be both faithful and virtuous?" When, Nandaka, a monk is both faithful and virtuous, then he is complete in that factor. Nandaka, a monk is faithful and virtuous, but he does not gain internal serenity of mind. ... [Pe] ... and gains internal serenity of mind, but he does not gain insight into the nature of things through higher wisdom. Thus, he is incomplete in that factor. Nandaka, just as if there were a four-footed animal, and one of its legs was stunted and defective, it would be incomplete in its limbs; in the same way, Nandaka, a monk is faithful, virtuous, and gains internal serenity of mind, but he does not gain insight into the nature of things through higher wisdom. Thus, he is incomplete in that factor. Therefore, he should fulfill that factor, thinking, "How can I be faithful, virtuous, gain internal serenity of mind, and also gain insight into the nature of things through higher wisdom?" When, Nandaka, a monk is faithful, virtuous, gains internal serenity of mind, and gains insight into the nature of things through higher wisdom, then he is complete in that factor.' Thus, he proclaimed the holy life, complete in all its parts and perfectly pure, through these four factors, and entered his dwelling.

Friends, there are these five benefits of hearing the Dhamma at the right time and discussing the Dhamma at the right time. What five? Here, friends, a monk teaches the Dhamma to the monks—the Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing; he proclaims the holy life, complete in all its parts and perfectly pure. Friends, in whatever way a monk teaches the Dhamma to the monks—the Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing, proclaiming the holy life...
172: ...whenever he explains the holy life that is entirely complete and pure, he becomes dear and pleasing to the Teacher, respected and esteemed. Friends, this is the first benefit of listening to the Dhamma at the proper time and discussing the Dhamma at the proper time. Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu teaches the Dhamma to bhikkhus—good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing; he explains the holy life that is entirely complete and pure. Friends, just as a bhikkhu teaches the Dhamma to bhikkhus... whenever he explains the holy life, he experiences the meaning and he experiences the Dhamma in that teaching. Friends, this is the second benefit of listening to the Dhamma at the proper time and discussing the Dhamma at the proper time. Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu teaches the Dhamma to bhikkhus—good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing; he explains the holy life that is entirely complete and pure. Friends, whenever a bhikkhu teaches the Dhamma to bhikkhus... whenever he explains the holy life, he sees the deep collection of meanings by penetrating them with wisdom. Friends, this is the third benefit of listening to the Dhamma at the proper time and discussing the Dhamma at the proper time. Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu teaches the Dhamma to bhikkhus—good in the beginning... he explains the holy life. Friends, whenever that bhikkhu teaches the Dhamma to bhikkhus... whenever he explains the holy life, his fellow practitioners praise him, saying: 'Surely this venerable one has attained [Arahantship] or is in the process of attaining it.' Friends, this is the fourth benefit of listening to the Dhamma at the proper time and discussing the Dhamma at the proper time. Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu teaches the Dhamma to bhikkhus—good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing; he explains the holy life that is entirely complete and pure. Friends, whenever a bhikkhu teaches the Dhamma to bhikkhus—good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing; whenever he explains the holy life that is entirely complete and pure, those bhikkhus therein who are trainees (sekhas), who have not yet attained their heart's desire but dwell aspiring for the unsurpassed security from bondage (Nibbāna), having heard that Dhamma, arouse energy for the attainment of the unattained...
173:
In that assembly, those monks who are Arahants, whose taints are destroyed, who have lived the holy life, done what had to be done, laid down the burden, reached their own goal, utterly destroyed the fetters of existence, and are completely liberated through final knowledge—having heard that Dhamma, they dwell devoted to a pleasant dwelling in this very life. Friends, this is the fifth benefit of listening to the Dhamma at the proper time and discussing the Dhamma at the proper time.

Friends, these are the five benefits of listening to the Dhamma at the proper time and discussing the Dhamma at the proper time.

The Fourth Sutta.

## 5 - Bala Sutta

5. Monks, there are these four powers. Which four? The power of wisdom (paññā-bala), the power of energy (viriya-bala), the power of blamelessness (anavajja-bala), and the power of sustainment (saṅgaha-bala).

And what, monks, is the power of wisdom? Here, monks, those things that are wholesome and reckoned as wholesome, those things that are unwholesome and reckoned as unwholesome, those things that are blameworthy and reckoned as blameworthy, those things that are blameless and reckoned as blameless, those things that are dark and reckoned as dark, those things that are bright and reckoned as bright, those things that should be cultivated and reckoned as such, those things that should not be cultivated and reckoned as such, those things that are not worthy of the noble ones and reckoned as such, those things that are worthy of the noble ones and reckoned as such—these things are well seen and well examined by that monk with wisdom. This, monks, is called the power of wisdom.

And what, monks, is the power of energy? Here, monks, for the abandoning of those things that are unwholesome and reckoned as unwholesome, those things that are blameworthy and reckoned as blameworthy, those things that are dark and reckoned as dark, those things that should not be cultivated and reckoned as such, those things that are not worthy of the noble ones and reckoned as such—he generates desire, makes an effort, arouses energy, exerts his mind, and strives. For the acquisition of those things that are wholesome and reckoned as wholesome, those things that are blameless and reckoned as blameless, those things that are bright and reckoned as bright, those things that should be cultivated and reckoned as such, those things that are worthy of the noble ones and reckoned as such—he generates desire, makes an effort, arouses energy, exerts his mind, and strives. This, monks, is called the power of energy.

And what, monks, is the power of blamelessness? Here, monks, a noble disciple is possessed of blameless bodily action, possessed of blameless verbal action, and possessed of blameless mental action. This, monks, is called the power of blamelessness.

And what, monks, is the power of sustainment? Monks, these are the bases of sustainment (saṅgahavatthu)—
174:
Giving (dāna),
endearing speech (peyyavajja),
beneficent conduct (atthacariyā),
and impartiality (samānattatā).
Monks, among gifts (dāna), the gift of the Dhamma (dhamma-dāna) is supreme. Monks, among endearing speech (peyyavajja), teaching the Dhamma repeatedly to one who is desirous and attentive is supreme. Monks, among beneficent conduct (atthacariyā), to exhort, settle, and establish one without faith in the perfection of faith; to exhort, settle, and establish one without virtue in the perfection of virtue... one who is stingy in the perfection of generosity (cāga)... one without wisdom in the perfection of wisdom is supreme. Monks, among impartiality (samānattatā), the impartiality of a Stream-enterer towards a Stream-enterer, of a Once-returner towards a Once-returner, of a Non-returner towards a Non-returner, and of an Arahant towards an Arahant is supreme. Monks, this nature of impartiality is called the power of sympathy (saṅgāhabala). Monks, these are the four powers.

Monks, a noble disciple possessed of these four powers has overcome five fears. What five? Fear of livelihood (ājīvikabhaya), fear of ill-repute (asilokabhaya), fear of embarrassment in assemblies (parisāsārajjabhaya), fear of death (maraṇabhaya), and fear of an unhappy destination (duggatibhaya).

Monks, that noble disciple reflects thus: 'I do not fear the fear of livelihood. Why should I fear the fear of livelihood? I have these four powers: the power of wisdom, the power of energy, the power of blamelessness, and the power of sympathy. One who is unwise might fear the fear of livelihood. One who is lazy might fear the fear of livelihood. One who is faulty in bodily, verbal, and mental actions might fear the fear of livelihood. One who is without sympathy might fear the fear of livelihood. I do not fear the fear of ill-repute. ...p... I do not fear the fear of embarrassment in assemblies. ...p... I do not fear the fear of death. ...p... I do not fear the fear of an unhappy destination (duggati). Why should I fear the fear of an unhappy destination? I have these four powers: the power of wisdom, the power of energy, the power of blamelessness, and the power of sympathy. One who is unwise might fear the fear of an unhappy destination. One who is lazy might fear the fear of an unhappy destination. One who is faulty in bodily, verbal, and mental actions might fear the fear of an unhappy destination. One who is without sympathy might fear the fear of an unhappy destination.' Monks, a noble disciple possessed of these four powers has overcome these five fears.

The Fifth Sutta.

## 6. Sevana Sutta

6. There, the Venerable Sāriputta addressed the monks. ...p...
175:
The Venerable Sāriputta said this: "Friends, a person is to be known in two ways: as one to be associated with and as one not to be associated with. Friends, robes are to be known in two ways: as those to be used and as those not to be used. Friends, almsfood is to be known in two ways: as that to be used and as that not to be used. Friends, lodgings are to be known in two ways: as those to be used and as those not to be used. Friends, a village or town is to be known in two ways: as one to be frequented and as one not to be frequented. Friends, a region is to be known in two ways: as one to be frequented and as one not to be frequented."

"'Friends, a person is to be known in two ways: as one to be associated with and as one not to be associated with.' In what connection was this said? Therein, when one knows of a person: 'While I associate with this person, unwholesome states increase and wholesome states decline; and the requisites of life to be provided by one who has gone forth—robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick—are obtained with difficulty; and the goal of the ascetic life for which I have gone forth from the home life into homelessness does not reach fulfillment through development,' then, friends, that person should depart from that individual, whether by night or by day, without taking leave; he should not be followed.

Therein, when one knows of a person: 'While I associate with this person, unwholesome states increase and wholesome states decline; but the requisites of life to be provided by one who has gone forth—robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick—are obtained without difficulty; yet the goal of the ascetic life for which I have gone forth from the home life into homelessness does not reach fulfillment through development,' then, friends, that person should depart from that individual, even without taking leave; he should not be followed.

Therein, when one knows of a person: 'While I associate with this person, unwholesome states decline and wholesome states increase; and the requisites of life to be provided by one who has gone forth—robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick—are obtained with difficulty; but the goal of the ascetic life for which I have gone forth from the home life into homelessness reaches fulfillment through development,'
176:
If one knows: 'For me, the benefit of this monkhood reaches growth and fulfillment,' then, friends, that person should follow that [other] person and not depart from them.

Among those persons, if one knows of a person: 'While I associate with this person, unwholesome states decline and wholesome states increase; and those requisites of life to be provided by one who has gone forth—robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick—are obtained by me without difficulty; and that purpose of monkhood for which I went forth from the home life into homelessness reaches growth and fulfillment,' then, friends, that person should follow that [other] person for as long as life lasts and should not depart, even if being driven away.

'Friends, a person is to be known in two ways: as one to be associated with and as one not to be associated with.' It is with reference to this that it was said.

'Friends, robes are to be known in two ways: as those to be used and as those not to be used.' With reference to what was this said? Among those robes, if one knows of a robe: 'While I use this robe, unwholesome states increase and wholesome states decline,' such a robe should not be used. Among those robes, if one knows of a robe: 'While I use this robe, unwholesome states decline and wholesome states increase,' such a robe should be used. 'Friends, robes are to be known in two ways: as those to be used and as those not to be used.' It is with reference to this that it was said.

## 7. Sutavā Sutta

7. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha on Mount Vulture Peak. Then the wanderer Sutavā approached the Blessed One and exchanged greetings with him. When they had concluded their greetings and cordial talk, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the wanderer Sutavā said to the Blessed One:

"Venerable sir, on one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling right here in Rājagaha at Giribbaja. There, venerable sir, I heard this from the Blessed One’s own lips, I received it from the Blessed One’s own lips: 'Sutavā, a monk who is an Arahant, one whose taints are destroyed, who has lived the holy life, done what had to be done, laid down the burden...'
178:
“...has attained his own goal, has destroyed the fetters of existence, and is liberated through right knowledge, such a monk is incapable of transgressing in five ways: A monk whose taints are destroyed is incapable of intentionally depriving a living being of life; a monk whose taints are destroyed is incapable of taking what is not given with the intent to steal; a monk whose taints are destroyed is incapable of engaging in sexual intercourse; a monk whose taints are destroyed is incapable of consciously telling a lie; a monk whose taints are destroyed is incapable of enjoying sensual pleasures by storing them up as he did formerly in the life of a householder.” (I have heard this from the presence of the Blessed One; I have received this from his presence.)

“How is it, Bhante? Was this well heard by me from the Blessed One, well received, well attended to, and well remembered?”

“Indeed, Sutavā, this was well heard by you, well received, well attended to, and well remembered. In the past, Sutavā, and also now, I speak thus: ‘A monk who is an Arahant, whose taints are destroyed, who has lived the holy life, done what was to be done, laid down the burden, attained his own goal, destroyed the fetters of existence, and is liberated through right knowledge, is incapable of transgressing in nine ways: A monk whose taints are destroyed is incapable of intentionally depriving a living being of life; a monk whose taints are destroyed is incapable of taking what is not given with the intent to steal; a monk whose taints are destroyed is incapable of engaging in sexual intercourse; a monk whose taints are destroyed is incapable of consciously telling a lie; a monk whose taints are destroyed is incapable of enjoying sensual pleasures by storing them up as he did formerly in the life of a householder; a monk whose taints are destroyed is incapable of following a wrong path through desire; a monk whose taints are destroyed is incapable of following a wrong path through hatred; a monk whose taints are destroyed is incapable of following a wrong path through delusion; a monk whose taints are destroyed is incapable of following a wrong path through fear.’

In the past, Sutavā, and also now, I speak thus: ‘A monk who is an Arahant, whose taints are destroyed, who has lived the holy life, done what was to be done, laid down the burden, attained his own goal, destroyed the fetters of existence, and is liberated through right knowledge, is incapable of transgressing in these nine ways.’”

The seventh sutta.

The eighth sutta.

## 9. Puggala Sutta

9. “Monks, there are these nine types of persons found existing in the world. Which nine? The Arahant, the one practicing for Arahantship, the Non-returner, the one practicing for the realization of the fruit of non-returning, the Once-returner,”
180:
...one practicing for the realization of the fruit of Once-returning, a Stream-enterer, one practicing for the realization of the fruit of Stream-entry, and a worldling (puthujjana). Monks, these nine persons are existing and found in the world.

The Ninth Sutta.

## 10. Āhuneyya Sutta
10. "Monks, these nine persons are worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, an unsurpassed field of merit for the world. Which nine? The Arahant, one practicing for Arahantship, the Non-returner, one practicing for the realization of the fruit of Non-returning, the Once-returner, one practicing for the realization of the fruit of Once-returning, the Stream-enterer, one practicing for the realization of the fruit of Stream-entry, and the Gotrabhū (one who has entered the lineage). Monks, these nine persons are worthy of gifts... an unsurpassed field of merit for the world."

The Tenth Sutta.

The first chapter, the Sambodhi Vagga, is finished.

## 2. Sīhanāda Vagga
## 1. Sīhanāda Sutta
11. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's monastery. Then the Venerable Sāriputta approached the Blessed One, prostrated himself, and sat down at one side. Sitting there, the Venerable Sāriputta said to the Blessed One: "Venerable Sir, I have completed the rains-residence in Sāvatthī. I wish, Venerable Sir, to depart for a tour of the country."

"Sāriputta, you may go when you think it is now the time (to do as you wish)."

Then the Venerable Sāriputta rose from his seat, prostrated himself before the Blessed One, and having performed the circumambulation, departed. Soon after the Venerable Sāriputta had left, a certain monk said to the Blessed One: "Venerable Sir, the Venerable Sāriputta, having struck me and without asking for forgiveness, has departed on a tour."

Then the Blessed One addressed a certain monk:
181:
"Come, monk, in my name tell Sāriputta: 'Friend Sāriputta, the Teacher calls you.'"

"Yes, Venerable Sir," that monk replied to the Blessed One, and he approached the Venerable Sāriputta and said: "Friend Sāriputta, the Teacher calls you."

"Yes, friend," the Venerable Sāriputta replied to that monk.

At that time, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna and the Venerable Ānanda, taking the keys, went around the dwellings, saying: "Come forth, venerable sirs! Come forth, venerable sirs! Now the Venerable Sāriputta will roar his lion's roar in the presence of the Blessed One."

Then the Venerable Sāriputta approached the Blessed One, prostrated himself, and sat down at one side. As the Venerable Sāriputta was sitting there, the Blessed One said to him: "Sāriputta, here a certain fellow monk has complained, saying: 'Venerable Sir, the Venerable Sāriputta, having struck me and without asking for forgiveness, has departed on a tour.'"

"Venerable Sir, only one in whom mindfulness directed to the body (kāyagatāsati) is not established in the body would strike a certain fellow monk and depart on a tour without asking for forgiveness.

"Venerable Sir, just as people throw clean things on the earth, and they throw unclean things, they drop excrement, they drop urine, they drop spit, they drop pus, and they drop blood, yet the earth is not repelled, humiliated, or disgusted by it; even so, Venerable Sir, I dwell with a mind like the earth—vast, exalted, measureless, without enmity, and without ill will. Venerable Sir, only one in whom mindfulness directed to the body is not established in the body would strike a certain fellow monk and depart on a tour without asking for forgiveness. (1)

"Venerable Sir, just as people wash clean things in water, and they wash unclean things, they wash away excrement, urine, spit, pus, and blood, yet the water is not repelled, humiliated, or disgusted by it; even so, Venerable Sir, I dwell with a mind like water—vast, exalted, measureless, without enmity, and without ill will. Venerable Sir, only one in whom mindfulness directed to the body is not established in the body would strike a certain fellow monk and depart on a tour without asking for forgiveness. (2)

"Venerable Sir, just as fire burns clean things, and it burns unclean things, it burns excrement, urine, spit, pus, and blood, yet the fire is not repelled, humiliated, or disgusted by it; even so, Venerable Sir, I dwell with a mind like fire—vast, exalted, measureless, without enmity, and without ill will. Venerable Sir, only one in whom mindfulness directed to the body is not established in the body would strike a certain fellow monk and depart on a tour without asking for forgiveness. (3)

"Venerable Sir, just as the wind blows over clean things, and it blows over unclean things, it blows over excrement, urine, spit, pus, and blood, yet the wind is not repelled, humiliated, or disgusted by it; even so, Venerable Sir, I dwell with a mind like the wind—vast, exalted, measureless, without enmity, and without ill will. Venerable Sir, only one in whom mindfulness directed to the body is not established in the body would strike a certain fellow monk and depart on a tour without asking for forgiveness. (4)",
182:
...burns blood as well. Just as fire is not repelled, humiliated, or disgusted by that burning, even so, Bhante, I dwell with a mind like fire—vast, exalted, immeasurable, without enmity, and without ill will. Indeed, Bhante, only one in whom mindfulness directed to the body is not established in the body might strike a fellow practitioner and depart on a journey without having asked for forgiveness. (3)
Bhante, just as the wind blows on clean things and also blows on unclean things—on feces, urine, saliva, pus, and blood—and the wind is not repelled, humiliated, or disgusted by that blowing, even so, Bhante, I dwell with a mind like the wind—vast, exalted, immeasurable, without enmity, and without ill will. Indeed, Bhante, only one in whom mindfulness directed to the body is not established in the body might strike a fellow practitioner and depart on a journey without having asked for forgiveness. (4)
Bhante, just as a dust-cloth wipes clean things and also wipes unclean things—on feces, urine, saliva, pus, and blood—and the dust-cloth is not repelled, humiliated, or disgusted by that wiping, even so, Bhante, I dwell with a mind like a dust-cloth—vast, exalted, immeasurable, without enmity, and without ill will. Indeed, Bhante, only one in whom mindfulness directed to the body is not established in the body might strike a fellow practitioner and depart on a journey without having asked for forgiveness. (5)
Bhante, just as an outcaste youth, boy or girl, holding a bowl and dressed in rags, enters a village or town with a humble mind, even so, Bhante, I dwell with a mind like an outcaste youth—vast, exalted, immeasurable, without enmity, and without ill will. Indeed, Bhante, only one in whom mindfulness directed to the body is not established in the body might strike a fellow practitioner and depart on a journey without having asked for forgiveness. (6)
Bhante, just as a bull with broken horns, gentle, well-tamed, and
183:
well-trained, wandering from street to street, from square to square, does not harm anything with its feet or horns, even so, Bhante, I dwell with a mind like a bull with broken horns—vast, exalted, immeasurable, without enmity, and without ill will. Indeed, Bhante, only one in whom mindfulness directed to the body is not established in the body might strike a fellow practitioner and depart on a journey without having asked for forgiveness. (7)
Bhante, just as a young woman or man, youthful and fond of ornaments, who has bathed their head, would be repelled, humiliated, and disgusted if the carcass of a snake, a dog, or a human were hung around their neck, even so, Bhante, I am repelled, humiliated, and disgusted by this foul body. Indeed, Bhante, only one in whom mindfulness directed to the body is not established in the body might strike a fellow practitioner and depart on a journey without having asked for forgiveness. (8)
Bhante, just as a man might carry a pot of fat that has many holes and is oozing and leaking from here and there, even so, Bhante, I carry this body that has many holes and is oozing and leaking from here and there. Indeed, Bhante, only one in whom mindfulness directed to the body is not established in the body might strike a fellow practitioner and depart on a journey without having asked for forgiveness.” (9)
Then that monk rose from his seat, arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, prostrated with his head at the Blessed One’s feet, and said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, a transgression has overcome me, such that I was foolish, confused, and unskilled, in that I accused the Venerable Sāriputta with what is untrue, empty, false, and non-existent. May the Blessed One accept my confession of this transgression as a transgression for the sake of future restraint.”
“Indeed, monk, a transgression has overcome you, such that you were foolish, confused, and unskilled, in that you accused Sāriputta with what is untrue, empty, false, and non-existent.
184:
"Monk, because you see your transgression as a transgression and make amends in accordance with the Dhamma, we accept it from you. For, monk, it is growth in the Discipline of the Noble One when one sees a transgression as a transgression, makes amends in accordance with the Dhamma, and practices restraint in the future."

Then the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Sāriputta: "Sāriputta, forgive this foolish man before his head splits into seven pieces right there."

"Venerable sir, I forgive that venerable one if he says to me, 'May that venerable one forgive me too,'" (he replied).

The first discourse.

## 2. Saupādisesa Sutta

12. At one time the Blessed One was staying at Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's Park. Then the Venerable Sāriputta, having dressed in the morning and taking his bowl and robe, entered Sāvatthī for alms. Then it occurred to the Venerable Sāriputta: "It is still too early to wander for alms in Sāvatthī. What if I were to approach the park of the wanderers of other sects?"

Then the Venerable Sāriputta approached the park of the wanderers of other sects. Having approached, he exchanged greetings with those wanderers of other sects. When they had concluded their courteous and memorable talk, he sat down to one side. At that time, among those wanderers of other sects who were sitting together and assembled, this chance conversation arose: "Friends, whoever dies with a residue remaining (saupādisesa), all of them are not released from hell, not released from the animal realm, not released from the sphere of afflicted spirits, not released from the plane of misery, the bad destination, the lower world."

Then the Venerable Sāriputta neither approved nor disapproved of the words of those wanderers of other sects. Without approving or disapproving, he rose from his seat and departed, thinking: "I will learn the meaning of this statement in the presence of the Blessed One."

Then the Venerable Sāriputta, having wandered for alms in Sāvatthī and returned from his alms round after his meal, approached the Blessed One. Having paid homage to him, he sat down to one side and said to the Blessed One: "Venerable sir, I dressed in the morning and, taking my bowl and robe, entered Sāvatthī for alms."
185:
"Venerable sir, it occurred to me: 'It is still too early to wander for alms in Sāvatthī. What if I were to approach the park of the wanderers of other sects?' Then, venerable sir, I approached the park of the wanderers of other sects. Having approached, I exchanged greetings with those wanderers of other sects. When we had concluded our courteous and memorable talk, I sat down to one side. At that time, among those wanderers of other sects who were sitting together and assembled, this chance conversation arose: 'Friends, whoever dies with a residue remaining, all of them are not released from hell, not released from the animal realm, not released from the sphere of afflicted spirits, not released from the plane of misery, the bad destination, the lower world.' Then, venerable sir, I neither approved nor disapproved of the words of those wanderers of other sects. Without approving or disapproving, I rose from my seat and departed, thinking: 'I will learn the meaning of this statement in the presence of the Blessed One.'"

"Sāriputta, who are these foolish and incompetent wanderers of other sects, that they would know who has a residue remaining as 'one with a residue remaining,' or who has no residue remaining as 'one with no residue remaining'?

Sāriputta, these nine persons, though dying with a residue remaining, are released from hell, released from the animal realm, released from the sphere of afflicted spirits, released from the plane of misery, the bad destination, the lower world. Which nine? Here, Sāriputta, a certain person is one who fulfills virtue, fulfills concentration, but practices only to a limited extent in wisdom (wisdom is not yet complete). With the destruction of the five lower fetters, he is one who attains Nibbāna in the interval (antarāparinibbāyī). This, Sāriputta, is the first person who, though dying with a residue remaining, is released from hell, released from the animal realm, released from the sphere of afflicted spirits, released from the plane of misery, the bad destination, the lower world. (1)

Furthermore, Sāriputta, here a certain person is one who fulfills virtue, fulfills concentration, but practices only to a limited extent in wisdom (wisdom is not yet complete),"
186:
That person, due to the destruction of the five lower fetters, is one who attains Nibbāna after having passed the middle of the lifespan (upahaccaparinibbāyī). ... is one who attains Nibbāna without exertion (asaṅkhāraparinibbāyī). ... is one who attains Nibbāna with exertion (sasaṅkhāraparinibbāyī). ... is one who goes upstream to the Akaniṭṭha realm (uddhaṃsoto akaniṭṭhagāmī). Sāriputta, this is the fifth person who, dying with residue remaining, is freed from hell, freed from the animal realm, freed from the sphere of peta, freed from the plane of misery, the bad destination, and the nether world. (2-5)

Sāriputta, furthermore, in this Dispensation, a certain person fulfills virtue, but practices only to a limited extent in concentration and wisdom (wisdom is not yet complete). With the destruction of the three fetters and the weakening of greed, hatred, and delusion, he is a Once-returner (sakadāgāmī) who, returning to this world only once, makes an end of suffering. Sāriputta, this is the sixth person who, dying with residue remaining, is freed from hell ... freed from the plane of misery, the bad destination, and the nether world. (6)

Sāriputta, furthermore, in this Dispensation, a certain person fulfills virtue, but practices only to a limited extent in concentration and wisdom (wisdom is not yet complete). With the destruction of the three fetters, he is a 'one-seeder' (ekabījī), who, having been reborn only once more in the human state, makes an end of suffering. Sāriputta, this is the seventh person who, dying with residue remaining, is freed from hell ... freed from the plane of misery, the bad destination, and the nether world. (7)

Sāriputta, furthermore, in this Dispensation, a certain person fulfills virtue, but practices only to a limited extent in concentration and wisdom (wisdom is not yet complete). With the destruction of the three fetters, he is one who goes from family to family (kolaṃkola), who, having wandered and roamed through two or three families, makes an end of suffering. Sāriputta, this is the eighth person who, dying with residue remaining, is freed from hell ... freed from the plane of misery, the bad destination, and the nether world. (8)

Sāriputta, furthermore, in this Dispensation, a certain person fulfills virtue, but practices only to a limited extent in concentration and wisdom (wisdom is not yet complete). With the destruction of the three fetters, he is one who is 'seven times at most' (sattakkhattuparama),
187:
who, having wandered and roamed through seven times at most among devas and humans, makes an end of suffering. Sāriputta, this is the ninth person who, dying with residue remaining, is freed from hell, freed from the animal realm, freed from the sphere of peta, freed from the plane of misery, the bad destination, and the nether world. (9)

Sāriputta, who are those foolish and incompetent wanderers of other sects that they should know who is 'with residue' as 'with residue' or who is 'without residue' as 'without residue'? Sāriputta, these are the nine persons who, dying with residue remaining, are freed from hell, freed from the animal realm, freed from the sphere of peta, freed from the plane of misery, the bad destination, and the nether world.

Sāriputta, I have not previously taught this Dhamma exposition to the monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen. For what reason? Lest they, having heard this Dhamma exposition, should fall into negligence. However, Sāriputta, I have spoken this Dhamma exposition in response to your question.

The Second Sutta.

## 4. Samiddhi Sutta

14. Then the Venerable Samiddhi approached the Venerable Sāriputta, and after paying homage, sat down at one side. As the Venerable Samiddhi was sitting there, the Venerable Sāriputta said this to him: “Friend Samiddhi, with what as object do a man’s thoughts and intentions arise?”

“Venerable sir, they arise with name-and-form (nāmarūpa) as object.”

“Samiddhi, where do those thoughts go to diversity?”
“Venerable sir, they go to diversity in the elements (dhātu).”

“Samiddhi, what is their origin?”
“Venerable sir, they have contact (phassa) as their origin.”

“Samiddhi, what is their meeting place?”
“Venerable sir, they have feeling (vedanā) as their meeting place.”

“Samiddhi, what is their head?”
“Venerable sir, they have concentration (samādhi) as their head.”

“Samiddhi, what is their dominance?”
“Venerable sir, they have mindfulness (sati) as their dominance.”

“Samiddhi, what is their supremacy?”
“Venerable sir, they have wisdom (paññā) as their supremacy.”

“Samiddhi, what is their essence?”
“Venerable sir, they have liberation (fruition) as their essence.”

“Samiddhi, in what are they immersed?”
“Venerable sir, they are immersed in the Deathless (Nirvana).”

## 5. Gaṇḍa Sutta

15. “Monks, suppose there were a boil (gaṇḍa) that had existed for many years. That boil would have nine openings, nine natural orifices. Whatever would discharge from it would be only what is impure, only what is foul-smelling, only what is loathsome.

“Monks, ‘boil’ is a name for this body, composed of the four great elements, born of mother and father, built up of rice and porridge, subject to impermanence, to being rubbed, massaged, breaking, and dissolution. Whatever discharges from it is only what is impure, only what is foul-smelling, only what is loathsome. Therefore, monks, be disenchanted with this body.”

## 6. Saññā Sutta

16. “Monks, these nine perceptions (saññā), when developed and cultivated, are of great fruit and great benefit, merging in the Deathless, ending in the Deathless. What nine?”
192:
What nine? The perception of unattractiveness (asubha-saññā), the perception of death (maraṇa-saññā), the perception of repulsiveness in food (āhāre paṭikūla-saññā), the perception of non-delight in the whole world (sabbaloke anabhirata-saññā), the perception of impermanence (anicca-saññā), the perception of suffering in the impermanent (anicce dukkha-saññā), the perception of non-self in suffering (dukkhe anatta-saññā), the perception of abandoning (pahāna-saññā), and the perception of dispassion (virāga-saññā).

## 10. Velāma Sutta

20. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍika approached the Blessed One, and after paying homage to him, sat down to one side. As the householder Anāthapiṇḍika was sitting there, the Blessed One said to him:

“Venerable Sir, alms-giving is practiced in my home, but it is only coarse broken rice with sour gruel as the second dish.”

“Householder, whether one gives coarse or fine alms, if one gives without respect, gives without heart, does not give with one's own hand, gives as if throwing it away, and gives without the view that there is a result of kamma—then, wherever the result of that gift arises, his mind does not incline to the enjoyment of excellent food, his mind does not incline to the enjoyment of excellent clothing, his mind does not incline to the enjoyment of excellent vehicles, and his mind does not incline to the enjoyment of the five excellent cords of sensual pleasure. Even his children, wife, slaves, messengers, and workers do not want to listen to him, do not lend an ear, and do not apply their minds to understand. Why is that? Because, householder, such is the result of deeds performed without respect.

“Householder, whether one gives coarse or fine alms, if one gives with respect, gives with heart, gives with one's own hand, does not give as if throwing it away, and gives with the view that there is a result of kamma—then, wherever the result of that gift arises, his mind inclines to the enjoyment of excellent food, his mind inclines to the enjoyment of excellent clothing, his mind inclines to the enjoyment of excellent vehicles, and his mind inclines to the enjoyment of the five excellent cords of sensual pleasure. Monks, how is an inferior man possessed of speed, but not of beauty, and not of proportions? For the third time, the Venerable Sāriputta said to the Venerable Candikaputta: "Friend Candikaputta, Devadatta does not teach the Dhamma to the bhikkhus thus: 'Friends, when a bhikkhu's mind is developed by the mind, it is fit for that bhikkhu to declare: "Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more for this state of being," so I understand.' "And how, friend, is a bhikkhu's mind well-developed by the mind? It is well-developed by the mind when he thinks, 'My mind is free from lust'; 'My mind is free from hatred'; 'My mind is free from delusion'; 'My mind is of a nature not subject to lust'; 'My mind is of a nature not subject to hatred'; 'My mind is of a nature not subject to delusion'; 'My mind is of a nature not returning to the realm of sensual desire'; 'My mind is of a nature not returning to the realm of form'; 'My mind is of a nature not returning to the formless realm.'

"Friend, for a bhikkhu whose mind is thus rightly liberated, even if powerful forms cognizable by the eye come into the range of the eye, they do not overwhelm his mind. His mind remains unmixed, steady, attained to imperturbability, and he observes their passing away.

"Friend, suppose there were a stone pillar sixteen cubits long, eight cubits of which were buried in the ground and eight cubits above the ground. Then, even if a powerful storm were to come from the east, it could not shake it, could not make it tremble. Even if it came from the west... from the north... from the south, it could not shake it, could not make it tremble. Why is that?"
205:
"Friend, it is because of the depth of the foundation and because the stone pillar is well-planted. In the same way, friend, for a bhikkhu whose mind is thus rightly liberated, even if powerful forms cognizable by the eye come into the range of the eye, they do not overwhelm his mind. His mind remains unmixed, steady, attained to imperturbability, and he observes their passing away.

"Even if powerful sounds cognizable by the ear... odors cognizable by the nose... tastes cognizable by the tongue... tactile objects cognizable by the body... mental phenomena cognizable by the mind come into the range of the mind, they do not overwhelm his mind. His mind remains unmixed, steady, attained to imperturbability, and he observes their passing away."

The sixth discourse.

## 7. Paṭhama Vera Sutta

27. Then the Blessed One addressed the householder Anāthapiṇḍika, who had approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side: "Householder, when five fears and enmities are stilled in a noble disciple, and he is possessed of the four factors of stream-entry, he may, if he wishes, declare of himself: 'I am one for whom hell is destroyed, the animal realm is destroyed, the sphere of pretas is destroyed, the plane of misery, the bad destination, the nether world are destroyed. I am a stream-enterer, no longer subject to perdition, assured, bound for enlightenment.'

"What are the five fears and enmities that are stilled? Householder, one who destroys life, by reason of destroying life, begets fear and enmity in the present life, begets fear and enmity in the future life, and experiences mental pain and grief. One who abstains from destroying life does not beget fear and enmity in the present life, does not beget fear and enmity in the future life, and does not experience mental pain and grief. Thus, for one who abstains from destroying life, that fear and enmity is stilled.

"Householder, one who takes what is not given... (etc.)... one who engages in sexual misconduct... one who speaks falsehood... one who drinks fermented and distilled liquors which are the basis for negligence, by reason of drinking fermented and distilled liquors which are the basis for negligence, begets fear and enmity in the present life, begets fear and enmity in the future life, and experiences mental pain and grief. One who abstains from fermented and distilled liquors which are the basis for negligence does not beget fear and enmity in the present life, does not beget fear and enmity in the future life, and does not experience mental pain and grief. Thus, for one who abstains from fermented and distilled liquors which are the basis for negligence, that fear and enmity is stilled. These five fears and enmities are stilled."
206:
With what four factors of stream-entry is one endowed? Householder, in this teaching, a noble disciple is endowed with confirmed confidence in the Buddha: 'The Blessed One is an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed trainer of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One.'

He is endowed with confirmed confidence in the Dhamma: 'The Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One, directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be personally experienced by the wise.'

He is endowed with confirmed confidence in the Saṅgha: 'The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing the good way, practicing the straight way, practicing the true way, practicing the proper way; that is, the four pairs of persons, the eight types of individuals; this Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, the unsurpassed field of merit for the world.'

He is endowed with virtues liked by the noble ones, unbroken, untorn, unblemished, unmottled, freeing, praised by the wise, ungrasped, leading to concentration. He is endowed with these four factors of stream-entry.

Householder, when these five dangers and enmities are stilled for a noble disciple, and he is endowed with these four factors of stream-entry, he may, if he wishes, declare of himself: 'I am one for whom hell is destroyed, the animal realm is destroyed, the realm of ghosts is destroyed, the plane of misery, the bad destination, and the nether world are destroyed. I am a stream-enterer, no longer bound for the nether world, fixed in destiny, with enlightenment as my destination.'
207:
The Seventh Sutta.

## 8. Second Sutta on Enmity (Dutiyavera Sutta)

28. Monks, when a noble disciple has stilled five dangers and enmities and is endowed with the four factors of stream-entry, he may, if he wishes, declare of himself: 'I am one for whom hell is destroyed, the animal realm is destroyed, the realm of ghosts is destroyed, the plane of misery, the bad destination, and the nether world are destroyed. I am a stream-enterer, no longer bound for the nether world, fixed in destiny, with enlightenment as my destination.'

What five dangers and enmities are stilled? Monks, whatever danger and enmity one who kills living beings produces in this life as a result of killing, and produces in the life to come, and whatever mental pain and grief he experiences; for one who abstains from killing... [etc.]... thus that danger and enmity is stilled.

Monks, whatever danger and enmity one who takes what is not given... [etc.]... one who drinks intoxicants such as wine and liquor that cause heedlessness produces in this life as a result of drinking intoxicants, and produces in the life to come, and whatever mental pain and grief he experiences; for one who abstains from intoxicants such as wine and liquor that cause heedlessness, he produces no danger and enmity in this life, nor in the life to come, and he does not experience mental pain and grief. For one who abstains from intoxicants such as wine and liquor that cause heedlessness, thus that danger and enmity is stilled. These five dangers and enmities are stilled.

With what four factors of stream-entry is he endowed? Here, monks, a noble disciple is endowed with confirmed confidence in the Buddha: 'The Blessed One is... [etc.]... teacher of devas and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One.' In the Dhamma... [etc.]... In the Saṅgha... [etc.]... He is endowed with virtues liked by the noble ones, unbroken, untorn, unblemished, unmottled, freeing, praised by the wise, ungrasped, leading to concentration. He is endowed with these four factors of stream-entry.

Monks, when these five dangers and enmities are stilled for a noble disciple, and he is endowed with these four factors of stream-entry, he may, if he wishes, declare of himself: 'I am one for whom hell is destroyed, the animal realm is destroyed, the realm of ghosts is destroyed, the plane of misery, the bad destination...'
208:
‘I am a stream-enterer, no longer subject to the nether world, fixed in destiny, with enlightenment as my destination.’

The eighth sutta.

## 9. Āghātavatthu Sutta
29. “Monks, there are these nine grounds for resentment. Which nine?
‘He has done me harm,’ one harbors resentment. ‘He is doing me harm,’ one harbors resentment. ‘He will do me harm,’ one harbors resentment.
‘He has done harm to one who is dear and agreeable to me,’ ... ‘He is doing harm,’ ... ‘He will do harm,’ one harbors resentment.
‘He has done good to one who is not dear and not agreeable to me,’ ... ‘He is doing good,’ ... ‘He will do good,’ one harbors resentment. Monks, these are the nine grounds for resentment.”

The ninth sutta.

## 10. Āghātapāṭivinaya Sutta
30. “Monks, there are these nine ways of removing resentment. Which nine? ‘He has done me harm; how could it be otherwise [to prevent it] in this person?’ thus one removes resentment. ‘He is doing me harm; how could it be otherwise in this person?’ thus one removes resentment. ‘He will do me harm; how could it be otherwise in this person?’ thus one removes resentment. ‘He has done harm to one who is dear and agreeable to me,’ ... ‘He is doing harm,’ ... ‘He will do harm; how could it be otherwise in this person?’ thus one removes resentment. ‘He has done good to one who is not dear and not agreeable to me,’ ... ‘He is doing good,’ ... ‘He will do good; how could it be otherwise in this person?’ thus one removes resentment. Monks, these are the nine ways of removing resentment.”

The tenth sutta.

## 11. Anupubbanirodha Sutta
31. “Monks, there are these nine successive cessations. Which nine? For one who has attained the first jhāna, the perception of sensuality ceases. For one who has attained the second jhāna, thought and examination cease. For one who has attained the third jhāna, rapture ceases. For one who has attained the fourth jhāna, in-and-out breathing ceases. For one who has attained the base of infinite space, the perception of form ceases.”
209:
“For one who has attained the base of infinite consciousness, the perception of the base of infinite space ceases. For one who has attained the base of nothingness, the perception of the base of infinite consciousness ceases. For one who has attained the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, the perception of the base of nothingness ceases. For one who has attained the cessation of perception and feeling, both perception and feeling cease. Monks, these are the nine successive cessations.”

The eleventh sutta.

The third chapter, the Sattāvāsavagga, is finished.

The summary of the chapter:
Three stations, the untrained horse, craving, seven, wisdom, the stone pillar, two on enmity, two on resentment, and successive cessations.

## 4. Mahāvagga
## 1. Anupubbavihāra Sutta
32. “Monks, there are these nine successive dwellings. Which nine? The first jhāna, the second jhāna, the third jhāna, the fourth jhāna, the base of infinite space, the base of infinite consciousness, the base of nothingness, the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, and the cessation of perception and feeling. Monks, these are the nine successive dwellings.”

The first sutta.

## 2. Anupubbavihārasamāpatti Sutta
33. “Monks, I will teach these nine successive attainments. Listen to that. ... And what, monks, are the nine successive attainments? In whatever place sensual pleasures cease, and those who dwell having repeatedly made sensual objects and sensual defilements cease—I say that those venerable ones are truly without hunger, extinguished, crossed over, and have reached the far shore by means of that [attainment]. If someone should say: ‘In what place do sensual pleasures cease, and which persons dwell having repeatedly made sensual pleasures cease? I do not know this, I do not see this,’ then he should be told: ‘Here, friend, a monk, secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by thought and examination, with rapture and happiness born of seclusion.’”
210:
“...enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is born of seclusion (from the hindrances) and accompanied by rapture (pīti) and pleasure (sukha). In this first jhāna, sensual desires (kāma) cease, and those persons dwell having repeatedly caused sensual desires to cease.” Monks, certainly an honest and sincere person would rejoice in and appreciate what is spoken as 'well said'. Having rejoiced in and appreciated what is spoken as 'well said', he would approach and attend to it with palms joined in reverence.

“In whatever place initial thought (vitakka) and sustained thought (vicāra) cease, and whoever dwells having repeatedly caused initial thought and sustained thought to cease, I say: 'Certainly those venerable ones are without hunger, extinguished, crossed over, and have reached the far shore by that factor (of the second jhāna).' If someone should say: 'In what place do initial thought and sustained thought cease? And who dwells having repeatedly caused initial thought and sustained thought to cease? I do not know this, I do not see this,' then he should be told: 'Here, friend, a bhikkhu, with the subsiding of initial and sustained thought... enters and dwells in the second jhāna. In this second jhāna, initial thought and sustained thought cease, and those (who have attained the second jhāna) dwell having repeatedly caused initial thought and sustained thought to cease.' Monks, certainly an honest and sincere person would rejoice in and appreciate what is spoken as 'well said'. Having rejoiced in and appreciated what is spoken as 'well said', he would approach and attend to it with palms joined in reverence.

“In whatever place rapture (pīti) ceases, and whoever dwells having repeatedly caused rapture to cease, I say: 'Certainly those venerable ones are without hunger, extinguished, crossed over, and have reached the far shore by that factor (of the jhāna).' If someone should say: 'In what place does rapture cease? And who dwells having repeatedly caused rapture to cease? I do not know this, I do not see this,' then he should be told: 'Here, friend, a bhikkhu, with the fading away of rapture... enters and dwells in the third jhāna. In this third jhāna, rapture ceases, and those (who have attained the third jhāna) dwell having repeatedly caused rapture to cease.' Monks, certainly an honest and sincere person would rejoice in and appreciate what is spoken as 'well said'. Having rejoiced in and appreciated what is spoken as 'well said', he would approach and attend to it with palms joined in reverence.

“In whatever place the pleasure of equanimity (upekkhā-sukha) ceases, and whoever dwells having repeatedly caused the pleasure of equanimity to cease, I say: 'Certainly those venerable ones are without hunger, extinguished, crossed over, and have reached the far shore by that factor (of the fourth jhāna).' If someone should say: 'In what place does the pleasure of equanimity cease? And who dwells having repeatedly caused the pleasure of equanimity to cease? I do not know this, I do not see this,' then he should be told: 'Here, friend, a bhikkhu, with the abandoning of pleasure...'
211:
“...enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna. In this fourth jhāna, the pleasure of equanimity (upekkhā-sukha) ceases, and those (who have attained the fourth jhāna) dwell having repeatedly caused the pleasure of equanimity to cease.' Monks, certainly an honest and sincere person would rejoice in and appreciate what is spoken as 'well said'. Having rejoiced in and appreciated what is spoken as 'well said', he would approach and attend to it with palms joined in reverence.

“In whatever place the perception of form (rūpasaññā) (arising from the kasina) ceases, and whoever dwells having repeatedly caused the perception of form to cease, I say: 'Certainly those venerable ones are without hunger, extinguished, crossed over, and have reached the far shore by that factor (of the jhāna).' If someone should say: 'In what place does the perception of form cease? And who dwells having repeatedly caused the perception of form to cease? I do not know this, I do not see this,' then he should be told: 'Here, friend, a bhikkhu, by completely transcending perceptions of form, with the disappearance of perceptions of sensory impact (paṭighasaññā), and by not attending to perceptions of diversity (nānattasaññā), thinking "space is infinite," enters and dwells in the base of infinite space (ākāsānañcāyatana).

In this (base of infinite space), those persons dwell having repeatedly caused the perception of form (rūpasaññā) to cease.' Monks, certainly an honest and sincere person would rejoice in and appreciate what is spoken as 'well said'. Having rejoiced in and appreciated what is spoken as 'well said', he would approach and attend to it with palms joined in reverence.

“In whatever place the perception of the base of infinite space (ākāsānañcāyatana-saññā) ceases, and whoever dwells having repeatedly caused the perception of the base of infinite space to cease, I say: 'Certainly those venerable ones are without hunger, extinguished, crossed over, and have reached the far shore by that factor (of the base of infinite consciousness).' If someone should say: 'In what place does the perception of the base of infinite space cease? And who dwells having repeatedly caused the perception of the base of infinite space to cease? I do not know this, I do not see this,' then he should be told: 'Here, friend, a bhikkhu, by completely transcending the base of infinite space, thinking "consciousness is infinite," enters and dwells in the base of infinite consciousness (viññāṇañcāyatana).

In this (base of infinite consciousness), the perception of the base of infinite space ceases, and those (who have attained the base of infinite consciousness) dwell having repeatedly caused the perception of the base of infinite space to cease.' Monks, certainly an honest and sincere person would rejoice in and appreciate what is spoken as 'well said'...”
212:
He should delight in and approve of the Dhamma spoken as "Excellent," and having delighted in and approved of it, he should pay homage and attend to it with joined palms.

"I say that in whatever place the perception of the base of infinite consciousness ceases, and whoever dwells having repeatedly made the perception of the base of infinite consciousness cease, those venerable ones are truly hungerless, attained to Nibbāna, crossed over, and gone to the further shore by that factor (of jhāna). If someone should say: 'In what place does the perception of the base of infinite consciousness cease, and who dwells having repeatedly made the perception of the base of infinite consciousness cease? I do not know this, I do not see this,' then he should be told: 'Here, friend, a bhikkhu, by completely transcending the base of infinite consciousness, enters and dwells in the base of nothingness, [thinking] "There is nothing." It is here that the perception of the base of infinite consciousness ceases, and they dwell having repeatedly made the perception of the base of infinite consciousness cease.'"

Monks, a person who is truly honest and without deceit would delight in and approve of what is spoken as "Excellent," and having delighted in and approved of it, he should pay homage and attend to it with joined palms.

"I say that in whatever place the perception of the base of nothingness ceases, and whoever dwells having repeatedly made the perception of the base of nothingness cease, those venerable ones are truly hungerless, attained to Nibbāna, crossed over, and gone to the further shore by that factor. If someone should say: 'In what place does the perception of the base of nothingness cease, and who dwells having repeatedly made the perception of the base of nothingness cease? I do not know this, I do not see this,' then he should be told: 'Here, friend, a bhikkhu, by completely transcending the base of nothingness, enters and dwells in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. It is here that the perception of the base of nothingness ceases, and they dwell having repeatedly made the perception of the base of nothingness cease.'"

Monks, a person who is truly honest and without deceit would delight in and approve of what is spoken as "Excellent," and having delighted in and approved of it, he should pay homage and attend to it with joined palms.

"I say that in whatever place the perception of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception ceases, and whoever dwells having repeatedly made the perception of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception cease, those venerable ones are truly hungerless, attained to Nibbāna, crossed over, and gone to the further shore by that factor (of the attainment of cessation). If someone should say: 'In what place does the perception of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception cease, and who dwells having repeatedly made the perception of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception cease? I do not know this, I do not see this,' then he should be told: 'Here, friend, a bhikkhu, by completely transcending the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, enters and dwells in the cessation of perception and feeling. It is here that the perception of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception ceases,"
213:
and they dwell having repeatedly made the perception of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception cease.' This is what should be said."

Monks, a person who is truly honest and without deceit would delight in and approve of what is spoken as "Excellent," and having delighted in and approved of it, he should pay homage and attend to it with joined palms. Monks, these are the nine successive meditative attainments.

The second discourse.

## 3. Nibbānasukha Sutta

34. On one occasion, the Venerable Sāriputta was staying at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels' Feeding Place. There, the Venerable Sāriputta addressed the bhikkhus: "Friends, this Nibbāna is happiness. Friends, this Nibbāna is happiness."

When this was said, the Venerable Udāyī said to the Venerable Sāriputta: "But friend Sāriputta, what happiness is there in this Nibbāna where there is no feeling?"

"Friend, just this is the happiness in this Nibbāna: that there is no feeling. Friend, there are these five cords of sensual pleasure. Which five?
