Forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust. Sounds cognizable by the ear... (p)... smells cognizable by the nose... tastes cognizable by the tongue... tactile objects cognizable by the body that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust. These, friend, are the five cords of sensual pleasure. The pleasure and joy that arise dependent on these five cords of sensual pleasure, this, friend, is called sensual pleasure (kāmasukha).

Here, friend, a bhikkhu, secluded from sensual pleasures... (p)... enters and dwells in the first jhāna.

Friend, if while he is dwelling in this attainment, perceptions and intentions accompanied by sensual desire occur to him, that is an affliction for him. Just as, friend, pain might arise in a happy person only to his affliction, so too, if perceptions and intentions accompanied by sensual desire occur to him, that is an affliction for him. Friend, whatever is an affliction, that the Blessed One has called suffering. In this way, friend, it should be understood how Nibbāna is happiness.

Furthermore, friend, with the subsiding of thought (vitakka) and examination (vicāra), a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the second jhāna. Friend, if while he is dwelling in this attainment, perceptions and intentions accompanied by thought occur to him, that is an affliction for him. Just as, friend, pain might arise in a happy person only to his affliction,"
214:
In the same way, friend, if perceptions and attentions accompanied by thought (vitakka) arise in that monk, that is an affliction for him. Friend, whatever is an affliction, the Blessed One has called it suffering. By this method, friend, it should be understood how Nibbāna is happiness.

Furthermore, friend, a monk, with the fading away of rapture (pīti)... enters and dwells in the third jhāna. Friend, if while he is dwelling in this state, perceptions and attentions accompanied by rapture arise in him, that is an affliction for him. Just as, friend, suffering might arise for a happy person only to his affliction, in the same way, if those perceptions and attentions accompanied by rapture arise in that monk, that is an affliction for him. Friend, whatever is an affliction, the Blessed One has called it suffering. By this method, friend, it should be understood how Nibbāna is happiness.

Furthermore, friend, a monk, with the abandoning of pleasure (sukha)... enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna. Friend, if while he is dwelling in this state, perceptions and attentions accompanied by equanimity (upekkhā) arise in him, that is an affliction for him. Just as, friend, suffering might arise for a happy person only to his affliction, in the same way, if those perceptions and attentions accompanied by equanimity arise in that monk, that is an affliction for him. Friend, whatever is an affliction, the Blessed One has called it suffering. By this method, friend, it should be understood how Nibbāna is happiness.

Furthermore, friend, a monk, by completely transcending perceptions of form (rūpasaññā), by the disappearance of perceptions of sensory impact (paṭighasaññā), and by not attending to perceptions of diversity (nānattasaññā), thinking 'space is infinite,' enters and dwells in the sphere of infinite space (ākāsānañcāyatana). Friend, if while he is dwelling in this state, perceptions and attentions accompanied by form arise in him, that is an affliction for him. Just as, friend, suffering might arise for a happy person only to his affliction, in the same way, if those perceptions and attentions accompanied by form arise in that monk, that is an affliction for him. Friend, whatever is an affliction, the Blessed One has called it suffering. By this method, friend, it should be understood how Nibbāna is happiness.
215:
Furthermore, friend, a monk, by completely transcending the sphere of infinite space, thinking 'consciousness is infinite,' enters and dwells in the sphere of infinite consciousness (viññāṇañcāyatana).

Friend, if while he is dwelling in this state, perceptions and attentions accompanied by the sphere of infinite space arise in him, that is an affliction for him. Just as, friend, suffering might arise for a happy person only to his affliction, in the same way, if those perceptions and attentions accompanied by the sphere of infinite space arise in him, that is an affliction for him. Friend, whatever is an affliction, the Blessed One has called it suffering. By this method, friend, it should be understood how Nibbāna is happiness.

Furthermore, friend, a monk, by completely transcending the sphere of infinite consciousness, thinking 'there is nothing,' enters and dwells in the sphere of nothingness (ākiñcaññāyatana). Friend, if while he is dwelling in this state, perceptions and attentions accompanied by the sphere of infinite consciousness arise in him, that is an affliction for him. Just as, friend, suffering might arise for a happy person only to his affliction, in the same way, if those perceptions and attentions accompanied by the sphere of infinite consciousness arise in him, that is an affliction for him. Friend, whatever is an affliction, the Blessed One has called it suffering. By this method, friend, it should be understood how Nibbāna is happiness.

Furthermore, friend, a monk, by completely transcending the sphere of nothingness, enters and dwells in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (nevasaññānāsaññāyatana). Friend, if while he is dwelling in this state, perceptions and attentions accompanied by the sphere of nothingness arise in him, that is an affliction for him. Just as, friend, suffering might arise for a happy person only to his affliction, in the same way, if those perceptions and attentions accompanied by the sphere of nothingness arise in him, that is an affliction for him. Friend, whatever is an affliction, the Blessed One has called it suffering. By this method, friend, it should be understood how Nibbāna is happiness.

Furthermore, friend, a monk, by completely transcending the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, enters and dwells in the cessation of perception and feeling (saññāvedayitanirodha). And having seen with wisdom, his taints (āsavas) are utterly destroyed. By this method, friend, it should be understood how Nibbāna is happiness.
216:
The Third Sutta.

## 4. Gāvī-upamā Sutta

35. "Monks, suppose there is a mountain cow, foolish, unskilled, ignorant of her pasture, and unskillful in roaming on rugged mountains. It might occur to her: 'What if I were to go to a region I have never been to before, eat grass I have never eaten before, and drink water I have never drunk before?' Without having placed her front foot firmly, she would lift her hind foot. That cow would not reach the region she had never been to before, nor eat the grass she had never eaten before, nor drink the water she had never drunk before. Moreover, she would not even return safely to the place where she had been standing when she thought: 'What if I were to go to a region I have never been to before... and drink water I have never drunk before?' Why is that? Because, monks, that mountain cow is foolish, unskilled, ignorant of her pasture, and unskillful in roaming on rugged mountains.

"In the same way, monks, here some monk is foolish, unskilled, ignorant of his pasture, and unskillful. Quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, he enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied thought (vitakka) and sustained thought (vicāra), with rapture (pīti) and happiness (sukha) born of seclusion. He does not pursue that sign (nimitta), does not develop it, does not cultivate it, and does not establish it well.

"It occurs to him: 'What if, with the subsiding of applied thought and sustained thought, I were to enter and dwell in the second jhāna, which has internal confidence and unification of mind, is without applied thought and sustained thought, and has rapture and happiness born of concentration (samādhi)?' He is unable, with the subsiding of applied thought and sustained thought... to enter and dwell in the second jhāna. Then it occurs to him: 'What if, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, I were to enter and dwell in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied thought and sustained thought, with rapture and happiness born of seclusion?' He is unable, quite secluded from sensual pleasures... to enter and dwell in the first jhāna. This monk, monks, is called one who has fallen away from both, who has failed in both, just like that mountain cow, foolish, unskilled, ignorant of her pasture, and unskillful in roaming on rugged mountains.

"Monks, suppose there is a mountain cow, wise, skilled, knowing her pasture, and skillful in roaming on rugged mountains. It might occur to her: 'What if I were to go to a region I have never been to before, eat grass I have never eaten before, and drink water I have never drunk before?' Having placed her front foot firmly, she would lift her hind foot. That cow would reach the region she had never been to before, eat the grass she had never eaten before, and drink the water she had never drunk before."
217:
And she would return safely to the place where she had been standing when she thought: 'What if I were to go to a region I have never been to before... and drink water I have never drunk before?' Why is that? Because, monks, that mountain cow is wise, skilled, knows her pasture, and is skillful in roaming on rugged mountains.

"In the same way, monks, here some monk is wise, skilled, knows his pasture, and is skillful. Quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, he enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied thought (vitakka) and sustained thought (vicāra), with rapture (pīti) and happiness (sukha) born of seclusion. He pursues that sign (nimitta), develops it, cultivates it, and establishes it well. It occurs to him: 'What if, with the subsiding of applied thought and sustained thought, I were to enter and dwell in the second jhāna... which has rapture and happiness born of concentration (samādhi)?' Without overreaching for the second jhāna, with the subsiding of applied thought and sustained thought, he enters and dwells in the second jhāna. He pursues that sign, develops it, cultivates it, and establishes it well.

"It occurs to him: 'What if, with the fading away as well of rapture, I were to dwell in equanimity (upekkhā), mindful (sato) and clearly comprehending (sampajāno), and experience happiness with the body, of which the noble ones declare: "He dwells happily in equanimity and mindfulness," and enter and dwell in the third jhāna?' Without overreaching for the third jhāna, with the fading away of rapture... he enters and dwells in the third jhāna. He pursues that sign, develops it, cultivates it, and establishes it well.

"It occurs to him: 'What if, with the abandoning of pleasure and pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, I were to enter and dwell in the fourth jhāna, which has neither-pain-nor-pleasure and has purity of mindfulness due to equanimity?' Without overreaching for the fourth jhāna, with the abandoning of pleasure... he enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna. He pursues that sign, develops it, cultivates it, and establishes it well.

"It occurs to him: 'What if, by completely transcending perceptions of form (rūpasaññā), with the disappearance of perceptions of sensory impact (paṭighasaññā), and by not attending to perceptions of diversity (nānattasaññā), thinking "space is infinite," I were to enter and dwell in the sphere of infinite space (ākāsānañcāyatana)?' Without overreaching for the sphere of infinite space, by completely transcending perceptions of form... he enters and dwells in the sphere of infinite space."
218:
That monk resorts to, develops, and cultivates that sign (of the sphere of infinite space), and establishes it well. It occurs to him: 'What if I, by completely transcending the sphere of infinite space, were to enter and dwell in the sphere of infinite consciousness, developing the thought "consciousness is infinite"?' Without harming the sphere of infinite consciousness, he completely transcends the sphere of infinite space and enters and dwells in the sphere of infinite consciousness, developing the thought 'consciousness is infinite'.

That monk resorts to, develops, and cultivates that sign (of the sphere of infinite consciousness), and establishes it well. It occurs to him: 'What if I, by completely transcending the sphere of infinite consciousness, were to enter and dwell in the sphere of nothingness, developing the thought "there is nothing"?' Without harming the sphere of nothingness, he completely transcends the sphere of infinite consciousness and enters and dwells in the sphere of nothingness, developing the thought 'there is nothing'. That monk resorts to, develops, and cultivates that sign (of the sphere of nothingness), and establishes it well.

It occurs to him: 'What if I, by completely transcending the sphere of nothingness, were to enter and dwell in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception?' Without harming the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, he completely transcends the sphere of nothingness and enters and dwells in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. That monk resorts to, develops, and cultivates that sign (of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception), and establishes it well. It occurs to him: 'What if I, by completely transcending the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, were to enter and dwell in the cessation of perception and feeling?' Without harming the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling, he completely transcends the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception and enters and dwells in the cessation of perception and feeling.

Bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu enters and emerges from these various attainments, his mind becomes soft and wieldy. With a mind that is soft and wieldy, immeasurable concentration is well-developed. With that immeasurable, well-developed concentration, he inclines his mind toward the realization by higher knowledge of whatever state is to be realized by higher knowledge. Whenever there is a basis (the preceding cause and the foundational jhāna of higher knowledge in this life), he attains the capacity to witness it in each case.

If he wishes: 'May I exercise the various kinds of supernormal powers: being one, may I become many; being many, may I become one... even as far as the Brahma world, may I exercise mastery with the body,' whenever there is a basis, he attains the capacity to witness it in each case.
219:
If he wishes: 'With the divine ear element...' ... whenever there is a basis, he attains the capacity to witness it in each case. If he wishes: 'May I understand the minds of other beings and persons, having encompassed them with my own mind. May I understand a mind with lust as a mind with lust; a mind without lust as a mind without lust; a mind with hate as a mind with hate; a mind without hate as a mind without hate; a mind with delusion as a mind with delusion; a mind without delusion as a mind without delusion; a contracted mind as a contracted mind; a distracted mind as a distracted mind; an exalted mind as an exalted mind; an unexalted mind as an unexalted mind; a surpassable mind as a surpassable mind;

an unsurpassable mind as an unsurpassable mind; a concentrated mind as a concentrated mind; an unconcentrated mind as an unconcentrated mind; a liberated mind as a liberated mind; and an unliberated mind as an unliberated mind,' whenever there is a basis, he attains the capacity to witness it in each case. If he wishes: 'May I recollect my manifold past lives, that is, one birth, two births... thus with their aspects and particulars, may I recollect my manifold past lives,' whenever there is a basis, he attains the capacity to witness it in each case. If he wishes: 'With the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans... may I understand beings faring according to their kamma,' whenever there is a basis, he attains the capacity to witness it in each case. If he wishes: 'By the destruction of the taints, may I, in this very life, through my own higher knowledge, realize and dwell in the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom,' whenever there is a basis, he attains the capacity to witness it in each case.
220:
Fourth Sutta.
## 5. Jhāna Sutta
36. "Monks, I say that the destruction of the taints (the fruit of Arahantship) is dependent on the first jhāna. I say that the destruction of the taints (the fruit of Arahantship) is dependent on the second jhāna. I say that the destruction of the taints (the fruit of Arahantship) is dependent on the third jhāna. I say that the destruction of the taints (the fruit of Arahantship) is dependent on the fourth jhāna. I say that the destruction of the taints (the fruit of Arahantship) is dependent on the base of infinite space. I say that the destruction of the taints (the fruit of Arahantship) is dependent on the base of infinite consciousness. I say that the destruction of the taints (the fruit of Arahantship) is dependent on the base of nothingness. I say that the destruction of the taints (the fruit of Arahantship) is dependent on the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. I say that the destruction of the taints (the fruit of Arahantship) is dependent on the attainment of cessation, which is the cessation of perception and feeling."
"'Monks, I say that the destruction of the taints (the fruit of Arahantship) is dependent on the first jhāna.' Thus it was said. In reference to what was this said?"
Monks, in this Dispensation, a monk, secluded from sensual pleasures... enters and dwells in the first jhāna. Whatever states are included therein—form, feeling, perception, volitional formations, and consciousness—he contemplates those states as impermanent, as suffering, as a disease, as a boil, as a dart, as misery, as an affliction, as alien, as disintegrating, as empty, and as non-self. He turns his mind away from those states. Having turned his mind away from those states, he directs his mind to the deathless element (Nibbāna): 'This is peaceful, this is sublime, that is, the stilling of all formations, the relinquishing of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, Nibbāna.' Standing there, he attains the destruction of the taints (the fruit of Arahantship). If he does not attain the destruction of the taints (the fruit of Arahantship), then by that very lust for the Dhamma, by that delight in the Dhamma, with the destruction of the five lower fetters, he becomes one of spontaneous birth, attaining final Nibbāna there, not subject to return from that world.
Monks, just as an archer or an archer's apprentice might practice on a straw man or a mound of clay, and later he becomes a long-distance shooter, a marksman who hits the target, and a piercer of a large body; even so, monks, a monk, secluded from sensual pleasures... enters and dwells in the first jhāna. Whatever states are included therein—form, feeling, perception, volitional formations, and consciousness—he contemplates those states as impermanent, as suffering, as a disease, as a boil, as a dart, as misery, as an affliction, as alien, as disintegrating, as empty, and as non-self.
221:
He turns his mind away from those states. Having turned his mind away from those states, he directs his mind to the deathless element (Nibbāna): 'This is peaceful, this is sublime, that is, the stilling of all formations, the relinquishing of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, Nibbāna.' Standing there, he attains the destruction of the taints (the fruit of Arahantship). If he does not attain the destruction of the taints (the fruit of Arahantship), then by that very lust for the Dhamma, by that delight in the Dhamma, with the destruction of the five lower fetters, he becomes one of spontaneous birth, attaining final Nibbāna there, not subject to return from that world. 'Monks, I say that the destruction of the taints (the fruit of Arahantship) is dependent on the first jhāna.' Thus it was said, and it was said in reference to this.
'Monks, I say that the destruction of the taints (the fruit of Arahantship) is dependent on the second jhāna. ... Monks, I say that the destruction of the taints (the fruit of Arahantship) is dependent on the third jhāna. ... Monks, I say that the destruction of the taints (the fruit of Arahantship) is dependent on the fourth jhāna.' Thus it was said. In reference to what was this said? Monks, in this Dispensation, with the abandoning of pleasure and pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, a monk enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna, which has neither-pain-nor-pleasure and has purity of mindfulness due to equanimity. Whatever states are included therein—form, feeling, perception, volitional formations, and consciousness—he contemplates those states as impermanent, as suffering, as a disease, as a boil, as a dart, as misery, as an affliction, as alien, as disintegrating, as empty, and as non-self. He turns his mind away from those states. Having turned his mind away from those states, he directs his mind to the deathless element (Nibbāna): 'This is peaceful, this is sublime, that is, the stilling of all formations, the relinquishing of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, Nibbāna.' Standing there, he attains the destruction of the taints (the fruit of Arahantship). If he does not attain the destruction of the taints (the fruit of Arahantship), then by that very lust for the Dhamma, by that delight in the Dhamma, with the destruction of the five lower fetters, he becomes one of spontaneous birth, attaining final Nibbāna there, not subject to return from that world.
Monks, just as an archer or an archer's apprentice might practice on a straw man or a mound of clay, and later he becomes a long-distance shooter, a marksman who hits the target, and a piercer of a large body; even so, monks, with the abandoning of pleasure... enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna.
222:
That bhikkhu, [regarding] the form, feeling... [and so on] in that fourth jhāna, is one who does not return from that world. 'Bhikkhus, I say that the destruction of the taints [the fruit of Arahantship] occurs in dependence on the fourth jhāna'—it was in reference to this that this was said.

'Bhikkhus, I also say that the destruction of the taints [the fruit of Arahantship] occurs in dependence on the base of infinite space (ākāsānañcāyatana)'—it was said. In reference to what was this said? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, with the complete surmounting of perceptions of form, with the passing away of perceptions of sensory impact, with non-attention to perceptions of diversity, aware that 'space is infinite,' enters and dwells in the base of infinite space. He contemplates those states—feeling, perception, volitional formations, and consciousness—that are included therein as impermanent, as suffering, as a disease, as a boil, as a dart, as misery, as an affliction, as alien, as disintegrating, as empty, and as non-self. He turns his mind away from those states. Having turned his mind away from those states, he directs his mind to the Deathless element (Nibbāna): 'This is peaceful, this is sublime, that is, the stilling of all formations, the relinquishing of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, Nibbāna.' Standing there, he attains the destruction of the taints.

If he does not attain the destruction of the taints, then through that very lust for the Dhamma, that delight in the Dhamma, with the destruction of the five lower fetters, he becomes one of spontaneous birth, attaining final Nibbāna there, not liable to return from that world. Bhikkhus, just as an archer or an archer's apprentice might practice on a straw figure or a mound of clay, and later on he becomes a long-distance shooter, a marksman who hits the target, and a piercer of great bodies; in the same way, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, with the complete surmounting of perceptions of form, with the passing away of perceptions of sensory impact, with non-attention to perceptions of diversity, aware that 'space is infinite,' enters and dwells in the base of infinite space. He [contemplates] those states—feeling, perception... [and so on]—that are included in that base of infinite space... and is one who does not return from that world. 'Bhikkhus, I say that the destruction of the taints occurs in dependence on the base of infinite space'—it was in reference to this that this was said.

'Bhikkhus, I say that [the destruction of the taints occurs] in dependence on the base of infinite consciousness... [and so on]... in dependence on the base of nothingness (ākiñcaññāyatana)'—it was said. In reference to what was this said? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, with the complete surmounting of the base of infinite consciousness...
223:
...surmounting [that], aware that 'there is nothing,' enters and dwells in the base of nothingness (ākiñcaññāyatana). He contemplates those states—feeling, perception, volitional formations, and consciousness—that are included in that base of nothingness as impermanent, as suffering, as a disease, as a boil, as a dart, as misery, as an affliction, as alien, as disintegrating, as empty, and as non-self. He turns his mind away from those states. Having turned his mind away from those states, he directs his mind to the Deathless element (Nibbāna): 'This is peaceful, this is sublime, that is, the stilling of all formations, the relinquishing of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, Nibbāna.' Standing there, he attains the destruction of the taints [the fruit of Arahantship]. If he does not attain the destruction of the taints, then through that very lust for the Dhamma, that delight in the Dhamma, with the destruction of the five lower fetters, he becomes one of spontaneous birth, attaining final Nibbāna there in that base of infinite consciousness, not liable to return from that Brahma world of infinite consciousness.

Bhikkhus, just as an archer or an archer's apprentice might practice on a straw figure or a mound of clay, and later on he becomes a long-distance shooter, a marksman who hits the target, and a piercer of great bodies; in the same way, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, with the complete surmounting of the base of infinite consciousness, aware that 'there is nothing,' enters and dwells in the base of nothingness. He contemplates those states—feeling, perception, volitional formations, and consciousness—that are included in that base of nothingness as impermanent, as suffering, as a disease, as a boil, as a dart, as misery, as an affliction, as alien, as disintegrating, as empty, and as non-self. He turns his mind away from those states.

Having turned his mind away from those states, he directs his mind to the Deathless element (Nibbāna): 'This is peaceful, this is sublime, that is, the stilling of all formations, the relinquishing of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, Nibbāna.' Standing there, he attains the destruction of the taints. If he does not attain the destruction of the taints, then through that very lust for the Dhamma, that delight in the Dhamma, with the destruction of the five lower fetters, he becomes one of spontaneous birth, attaining final Nibbāna there in that base of nothingness, not liable to return from that Brahma world of nothingness. 'Bhikkhus, I say that the destruction of the taints occurs in dependence on the base of nothingness'—it was in reference to this aforementioned reason that this was said. Thus, bhikkhus, as far as there is attainment with perception, there is penetration to final knowledge.
224:
"Monks, regarding these two attainments—the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception and the cessation of perception and feeling—which are based on these lower jhānas, I say that those meditators who are skilled in entering attainments and skilled in emerging from attainments, having entered and emerged, are well-spoken of and praised (as peaceful and sublime)."

The Fifth Sutta.

## 6. Ānanda Sutta

37. At one time, the Venerable Ānanda was staying at Kosambī in Ghosita’s Park. There, the Venerable Ānanda addressed the monks: "Friends, monks!" "Friend," those monks replied to the Venerable Ānanda. The Venerable Ānanda said this:

"It is wonderful, friends! It is amazing, friends! How this Blessed One, who knows and sees, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, has discovered the attainment of an opening in the midst of confinement for the purification of beings, for the overcoming of sorrow and lamentation, for the disappearance of pain and displeasure, for the attainment of the true method, and for the realization of Nibbāna. While that very eye exists and those forms are present, one does not experience that sense base. While that very ear exists and those sounds are present, one does not experience that sense base. While that very nose exists and those odors are present, one does not experience that sense base. While that very tongue exists and those tastes are present, one does not experience that sense base. While that very body exists and those tactile objects are present, one does not experience that sense base."

When this was said, the Venerable Udāyī said to the Venerable Ānanda: "Friend Ānanda, is it while one is conscious that one does not experience that sense base, or while one is unconscious?" "Friend, it is while one is conscious that one does not experience that sense base, not while one is unconscious."

"But with what perception, friend, does one not experience that sense base while being conscious?"

"Here, friend, a monk, by completely transcending perceptions of form, by the disappearance of perceptions of sensory reaction, and by non-attention to perceptions of diversity, thinking 'Space is infinite,' enters and dwells in the sphere of infinite space. Being thus conscious, friend, one does not experience that sense base."
225:
"Furthermore, friend, a monk, by completely transcending the sphere of infinite space, thinking 'Consciousness is infinite,' enters and dwells in the sphere of infinite consciousness. Being thus conscious, friend, one does not experience that sense base."

"Furthermore, friend, a monk, by completely transcending the sphere of infinite consciousness, thinking 'There is nothing,' enters and dwells in the sphere of nothingness. Being thus conscious, friend, one does not experience that sense base."

"Once, friend, I was staying at Sāketa in the Anjana Wood, the Deer Park. Then, friend, a nun who lived in Jaṭila approached me, paid homage to me, and stood to one side. Standing to one side, that nun who lived in Jaṭila said to me: 'Venerable Ānanda, this concentration which does not lean forward (due to lust) and does not lean back (due to hatred), which is not maintained by forceful suppression, which is stable because of liberation, content because of stability, and not agitated because of contentment—what did the Blessed One say is the fruit of this concentration?'"

"When this was said, friend, I said to that nun who lived in Jaṭila: 'Sister, this concentration which does not lean forward and does not lean back, which is not maintained by forceful suppression, which is stable because of liberation, content because of stability, and not agitated because of contentment—the Blessed One said that the fruit of this concentration is final knowledge (Arahantship).' Being thus conscious, friend, one does not experience that sense base."

The Sixth Sutta.

## 7. Lokāyatika Sutta

38. Then two Brahmins who were cosmologists (Lokāyatikas) approached the Blessed One. Having approached, they exchanged greetings with the Blessed One. When they had concluded their greetings and cordial talk, they sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, those Brahmins said to the Blessed One:

"Master Gotama, Pūraṇa Kassapa is all-knowing and all-seeing; he claims to have complete knowledge and vision, saying: 'Whether I am walking, standing, sleeping, or awake, knowledge and vision are constantly and continuously present to me.'"
226:
That Pūraṇa Kassapa says: 'With infinite knowledge, I dwell knowing and seeing the infinite world.' Venerable Gotama, this Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta also claims to be all-knowing and all-seeing, professing complete knowledge and vision: 'Whether I am walking, standing, sleeping, or awake, knowledge and vision are constantly and continuously present to me.' He says: 'With infinite knowledge, I dwell knowing and seeing the infinite world.' Venerable Gotama, of these two who claim such knowledge and hold views that contradict each other, who speaks the truth and who speaks falsely?

Enough, Brahmins! Let it be: 'Of these two who claim such knowledge and hold views that contradict each other, who speaks the truth and who speaks falsely.' I will teach you the Dhamma, Brahmins. Listen to it and pay close attention; I will speak.

"Yes, Bhante," those Brahmins replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:

Brahmins, suppose there were four men standing in the four directions, endowed with supreme speed and a supreme stride. They might have such speed as a skilled archer, trained, practiced, and experienced, who could easily shoot a light arrow across the shadow of a palm tree. And they might have such a stride that it could reach from the eastern ocean to the western ocean. Then the man standing in the eastern direction might say: 'I will reach the end of the world by traveling.' Except for the time taken for eating, drinking, chewing, and tasting, for voiding excrement and urine, and for sleep and relieving fatigue, though he has a lifespan of a hundred years and lives for a hundred years, he would die along the way after traveling for a hundred years without reaching the end of the world. Then the man standing in the western direction... [as above] ...the northern direction... the southern direction... the man standing in the southern direction might say: 'I will reach the end of the world by traveling.' Except for the time taken for eating, drinking, chewing, and tasting, for voiding excrement and urine, and for sleep and relieving fatigue, though he has a lifespan of a hundred years and lives for a hundred years, he would die along the way after traveling for a hundred years without reaching the end of the world.
227:
Why is that? Brahmins, I do not say that the end of the world can be known, seen, or reached by such traveling. Yet, Brahmins, I also do not say that the end of suffering can be made without reaching the end of the world.

Brahmins, these five cords of sensual pleasure are called 'the world' in the Noble Discipline (the Buddha's teaching). Which five? Forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust. Sounds cognizable by the ear... [etc.] ...Odors cognizable by the nose... Tastes cognizable by the tongue... Tangibles cognizable by the body that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust. Brahmins, these five cords of sensual pleasure are called 'the world' in the Noble Discipline.

Brahmins, here a monk, secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by initial thought (vitakka) and sustained thought (vicāra), with rapture (pīti) and happiness (sukha) born of seclusion. Brahmins, this monk is said to have reached the end of the world and to dwell at the end of the world. Yet others say of him: 'This one is still included in the world; he has not yet escaped from the world.' And I too, Brahmins, say: 'This one is still included in the world; he has not yet escaped from the world.'

Furthermore, Brahmins, with the subsiding of initial and sustained thought... [etc.] ...the second jhāna... the third jhāna... the fourth jhāna... enters and dwells. Brahmins, this monk is said to have reached the end of the world and to dwell at the end of the world. Yet others say of him: 'This one is still included in the world; he has not yet escaped from the world.' And I too, Brahmins, say: 'This one is still included in the world; he has not yet escaped from the world.'

Furthermore, Brahmins, by completely transcending perceptions of form, with the passing away of perceptions of sensory impact, and by not attending to perceptions of diversity, [perceiving] 'space is infinite,' a monk enters and dwells in the sphere of infinite space (ākāsānañcāyatana).
228:
"Brahmins, this monk is said to have reached the end of the world and to dwell at the end of the world. Others say of him: 'This one too is included in the world; this one too has not yet escaped from the world.' Brahmins, I too say: 'This one too is included in the world; this one too has not yet escaped from the world.'

Brahmins, furthermore, a monk, having completely transcended the sphere of infinite space, [perceiving] 'consciousness is infinite,' enters and dwells in the sphere of infinite consciousness. ... Having completely transcended the sphere of infinite consciousness, [perceiving] 'there is nothing,' enters and dwells in the sphere of nothingness. ... Having completely transcended the sphere of nothingness, enters and dwells in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. Brahmins, this monk is said to have reached the end of the world and to dwell at the end of the world. Others say of him: 'This one too is included in the world; this one too has not yet escaped from the world.' Brahmins, I too say: 'This one too is included in the world; this one too has not yet escaped from the world.' Brahmins, furthermore, a monk, having completely transcended the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, enters and dwells in the cessation of perception and feeling. And having seen with wisdom, his taints (āsavas) are utterly destroyed. Brahmins, this monk is said to have reached the end of the world and to dwell at the end of the world, having crossed over the entanglement (visattika) in the world."

Seventh Sutta.

## 8. Devāsurasaṅgāma Sutta

39. Monks, in the past, a battle was arrayed between the Devas and the Asuras. Monks, in that battle, the Asuras won and the Devas were defeated. Monks, the defeated Devas fled only towards the north, and the Asuras pursued them. Monks, then the Devas thought: 'The Asuras are pursuing us. What if we were to fight the Asuras a second time?' Monks, for a second time, the Devas fought with the Asuras. Monks, for a second time, the Asuras won and the Devas were defeated. The defeated Devas fled only towards the north, and the Asuras pursued them. Monks, then the Devas thought: 'The Asuras are pursuing us. What if we were to fight the Asuras a third time?' Monks, for a third time, the Devas fought with the Asuras. Monks, for a third time, the Asuras won and the Devas were defeated.
229:
Monks, the defeated Devas, being afraid, entered only the city of the Devas (Tāvatiṃsa). Monks, to the Devas who had returned to the city of the Devas, this thought occurred: 'Now we dwell with ourselves having reached a place of safety from fear; the Asuras can do nothing to us.' Monks, to the Asuras also, this thought occurred: 'Now the Devas dwell with themselves having reached a place of safety from fear; we can do nothing to them.'

Monks, in the past, a battle was arrayed between the Devas and the Asuras. Monks, in that battle, the Devas won and the Asuras were defeated. Monks, the defeated Asuras fled only towards the south, and the Devas pursued them. Monks, then the Asuras thought: 'The Devas are pursuing us. What if we were to fight the Devas a second time?' Monks, for a second time, the Asuras fought with the Devas. Monks, for a second time, the Devas won and the Asuras were defeated. The defeated Asuras fled only towards the south, and the Devas pursued them. Monks, then the Asuras thought: 'The Devas are pursuing us. What if we were to fight the Devas a third time?' Monks, for a third time, the Asuras fought with the Devas. Monks, for a third time, the Devas won and the Asuras were defeated. Monks, the defeated Asuras, being afraid, entered only the city of the Asuras. Monks, to the Asuras who had returned to the city of the Asuras, this thought occurred: 'Now we dwell with ourselves having reached a place of safety from fear; the Devas can do nothing to us.' Monks, to the Devas also, this thought occurred: 'Now the Asuras dwell with themselves having reached a place of safety from fear; we can do nothing to them.'

In the same way, monks, at whatever time a monk, secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied thought (vitakka) and sustained thought (vicāra), with rapture (pīti) and happiness (sukha) born of seclusion. At that time, monks, the thought occurs to the monk: 'Now I dwell with myself having reached a place of safety from fear; Māra can do nothing to me.'
230:
Monks, to Māra the Evil One, it also occurs: 'Now this monk dwells with a body that has reached safety from danger; he is one I can do nothing to.'

Monks, at the time when a monk, with the subsiding of applied thought (vitakka) and sustained thought (vicāra)... [pe]... enters and dwells in the second jhāna... the third jhāna... the fourth jhāna. At that time, it occurs to the monk: 'Now I dwell with a body that has reached safety from danger; Māra can do nothing to me.' Monks, to Māra the Evil One, it also occurs: 'Now this monk dwells with a body that has reached safety from danger; he is one I can do nothing to.'

Monks, at the time when a monk, by completely surmounting perceptions of form (rūpasaññā), by the disappearance of perceptions of sensory impact (paṭighasaññā), and by non-attention to perceptions of diversity (nānattasaññā), thinking 'Space is infinite,' enters and dwells in the base of infinite space (ākāsānañcāyatana). Monks, this is called a monk who has made an end of Māra, who, having destroyed Māra's eye without a trace, has gone to where the Evil One cannot see him, and has crossed over the attachment (taṇhā) in the world.

Monks, at the time when a monk, by completely surmounting the base of infinite space, thinking 'Consciousness is infinite,' enters and dwells in the base of infinite consciousness (viññāṇañcāyatana)... by completely surmounting the base of infinite consciousness, thinking 'There is nothing,' enters and dwells in the base of nothingness (ākiñcaññāyatana)... by completely surmounting the base of nothingness, enters and dwells in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (nevasaññānāsaññāyatana)... by completely surmounting the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, enters and dwells in the cessation of perception and feeling (saññāvedayitanirodha), and having seen with wisdom, his taints (āsavas) are destroyed. Monks, this is called a monk who has made an end of Māra, who, having destroyed Māra's eye without a trace, has gone to where the Evil One cannot see him, and has crossed over the attachment (taṇhā) in the world.

The eighth discourse.

## 9. Nāga Sutta

40. Monks, at the time when a forest bull elephant, while going to his feeding ground, is preceded by bull calves, female elephants, young elephants, and nursing calves who break off the tips of the grass. Monks, at that time, the forest bull elephant is troubled, ashamed, and disgusted. Monks, at the time when a forest bull elephant, while going to his feeding ground, has the branches he has broken and pulled down eaten by bull calves, female elephants, young elephants, and nursing calves. Monks, at that time, the forest bull elephant is troubled...
231:
...ashamed, and disgusted. Monks, at the time when a forest bull elephant, whether descending to or ascending from the watering place, is preceded by bull calves, female elephants, young elephants, and nursing calves who stir up the water with their trunks. Monks, at that time, the forest bull elephant is troubled, ashamed, and disgusted. Monks, at the time when a forest bull elephant, whether descending to or ascending from the watering place, has female elephants go along rubbing against his body. Monks, at that time, the forest bull elephant is troubled, ashamed, and disgusted.

Monks, at that time, it occurs to the forest bull elephant: 'Now I dwell crowded with bull calves, female elephants, young elephants, and nursing calves. I eat grass with broken tips, and they eat the branches I have broken and pulled down. I drink muddy water, and when I descend to or ascend from the watering place, the female elephants go along rubbing against my body. What if I were to dwell alone, withdrawn from the herd?'

Later, he dwells alone, withdrawn from the herd. He eats grass with unbroken tips, they do not eat the branches he has broken and pulled down, he drinks clear water, and when he descends to or ascends from the watering place, the female elephants do not go along rubbing against his body.

Monks, at that time, it occurs to the forest bull elephant: 'Formerly, I dwelt crowded with bull calves, female elephants, young elephants, and nursing calves. I ate grass with broken tips, and they ate the branches I had broken and pulled down. I drank muddy water, and when I descended to or ascend from the watering place, the female elephants went along rubbing against my body. Now I dwell alone, without a companion, withdrawn from the herd. I eat grass with unbroken tips, they do not eat the branches I have broken and pulled down, I drink clear water, and when I descend to or ascend from the watering place, the female elephants do not go along rubbing against my body.'

That bull elephant, having broken a branch with his trunk and massaged his body with it, being delighted, raises his trunk.

Monks, in the same way, at the time when a monk dwells crowded with monks, nuns, laymen, laywomen, kings, royal ministers, sectarians, and disciples of sectarians. Monks, at that time, it occurs to the monk: 'Now I dwell crowded with monks, nuns, laymen, laywomen, kings, royal ministers, sectarians, and disciples of sectarians...'
232:
'It would be good if I were to live alone, withdrawn from the group.' That monk resorts to a secluded lodging—a forest, the foot of a tree, a mountain, a cleft, a mountain cave, a cemetery, a woodland thicket, the open air, or a heap of straw. Having gone to the forest, the foot of a tree, or an empty hut, he sits down, having folded his legs crosswise, set his body erect, and established mindfulness in front of him.

Abandoning covetousness (abhijjhā) for the world, he dwells with a mind free from covetousness; he purifies his mind from covetousness. Abandoning ill-will and malice, he dwells with a mind free from ill-will, sympathetic to the welfare of all living beings; he purifies his mind from ill-will and malice. Abandoning sloth and torpor (thina-middha), he dwells free from sloth and torpor, perceiving light, mindful and clearly comprehending; he purifies his mind from sloth and torpor. Abandoning restlessness (uddhacca) and remorse (kukkucca), he dwells without agitation, with a mind inwardly peaceful; he purifies his mind from restlessness and remorse. Abandoning doubt (vicikicchā), he dwells having crossed over doubt, without perplexity regarding wholesome states; he purifies his mind from doubt.

Having abandoned these five hindrances (nīvaraṇa), imperfections of the mind that weaken wisdom, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, he enters and dwells in the first jhana, which is accompanied by thought (vitakka) and examination (vicāra), with rapture (pīti) and happiness (sukha) born of seclusion. Being gratified, he draws in his trunk [meaning: he removes the suffering of defilements which is like an itch]. With the subsiding of thought and examination... [pe]... he enters and dwells in the second jhana... the third jhana... the fourth jhana. Being gratified, he draws in his trunk.

With the complete surmounting of perceptions of form (rūpasaññā), with the passing away of perceptions of sensory impingement (paṭighasaññā), with non-attention to perceptions of diversity (nānattasaññā), aware that 'space is infinite,' he enters and dwells in the sphere of infinite space (ākāsānañcāyatana). Being gratified, he draws in his trunk. With the complete surmounting of the sphere of infinite space, aware that 'consciousness is infinite,' he enters and dwells in the sphere of infinite consciousness (viññāṇañcāyatana)... With the complete surmounting of the sphere of infinite consciousness, aware that 'there is nothing,' he enters and dwells in the sphere of nothingness (ākiñcaññāyatana)... With the complete surmounting of the sphere of nothingness, he enters and dwells in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (nevasaññānāsaññāyatana).
233:
With the complete surmounting of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, he enters and dwells in the cessation of perception and feeling (saññāvedayitanirodha). Having seen with wisdom, his taints (āsava) are utterly destroyed. Being gratified, he draws in his trunk.

The Ninth Sutta.

## 10. Tapussa Sutta

41. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling among the Mallans at a town of the Mallans named Uruvelakappa. Then, in the morning, the Blessed One dressed, took his bowl and outer robe, and entered Uruvelakappa for alms. Having walked for alms in Uruvelakappa, after the meal, when he had returned from his alms round, he addressed the Venerable Ānanda: 'Stay here for a while, Ānanda, while I enter the Great Wood (Mahāvana) for the day's abiding.'

'Yes, Bhante,' the Venerable Ānanda replied to the Blessed One. Then the Blessed One entered the Great Wood and sat down at the foot of a certain tree for the day's abiding. Then Tapussa the householder approached the Venerable Ānanda, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. Sitting there, Tapussa the householder said to the Venerable Ānanda:

'Bhante Ānanda, we are laypeople who enjoy sensual pleasures, delighting in sensual pleasures, rejoicing in sensual pleasures, and finding joy in sensual pleasures. To us laypeople who enjoy sensual pleasures... renunciation (nekkhamma) seems like a steep precipice. Bhante, I have heard this: "In this Dhamma-Vinaya, the minds of very young monks leap forward into renunciation, find confidence in it, stand firm in it, and are released in it, seeing it as peaceful." Bhante, in this Dhamma-Vinaya, this renunciation of the monks is quite different from that of the manyfolk.'

'Householder, this is a worthy topic of conversation to present to the Blessed One. Come, householder, let us approach the Blessed One. Having approached him, we will report this matter to the Blessed One. As the Blessed One explains it to us, so shall we bear it in mind.'

'Yes, Bhante,' Tapussa the householder replied to the Venerable Ānanda.
234:
Then the Venerable Ānanda, together with Tapussa the householder, approached the Blessed One. Having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One:

“Venerable Sir, this Tapussa the householder said to me: ‘Venerable Ānanda, we are householders who enjoy sensual pleasures, who delight in sensual pleasures, who rejoice in sensual pleasures, who are thrilled by sensual pleasures. To us householders who enjoy, delight in, rejoice in, and are thrilled by sensual pleasures, renunciation (nekkhamma) appears like a precipice. Venerable Sir, I have heard that in this Dhamma-Vinaya, the minds of very young monks leap forward to renunciation, are confident in it, become established in it, and are released in it, seeing it as peaceful. Venerable Sir, this renunciation of the monks in this Dhamma-Vinaya is quite different from that of the manyfolk.’

“So it is, Ānanda! So it is, Ānanda! Before my enlightenment, Ānanda, while I was still an unenlightened Bodhisatta, the thought occurred to me: ‘Renunciation is good; seclusion is good.’ But my mind did not leap forward to renunciation, was not confident in it, did not become established in it, and was not released in it, seeing it as peaceful. Then, Ānanda, the thought occurred to me: ‘What is the cause, what is the reason, why my mind does not leap forward to renunciation, is not confident in it, does not become established in it, and is not released in it, seeing it as peaceful?’ Then, Ānanda, the thought occurred to me: ‘I have not seen the danger in sensual pleasures, nor have I cultivated that [vision]; I have not realized the benefit of renunciation, nor have I pursued it. Therefore, my mind does not leap forward to renunciation, is not confident in it, does not become established in it, and is not released in it, seeing it as peaceful.’

“Then, Ānanda, the thought occurred to me: ‘If I were to see the danger in sensual pleasures and cultivate that [vision], and if I were to realize the benefit of renunciation and pursue it, then it is possible that my mind would leap forward to renunciation, be confident in it, become established in it, and be released in it, seeing it as peaceful.’ Then, Ānanda, at a later time, having seen the danger in sensual pleasures, I cultivated that [vision]; having realized the benefit of renunciation, I pursued it. Then, Ānanda, my mind leaped forward to renunciation, was confident in it, became established in it, and was released in it, seeing it as peaceful.

“Then, Ānanda, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, I entered and dwelt in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by thought (vitakka) and examination (vicāra), with rapture (pīti) and happiness (sukha) born of seclusion. While I was dwelling in this state, Ānanda, perceptions and intentions accompanied by sensual desire occurred to me. That was an affliction for me.”
235:
“Ānanda, just as pain might arise for a person who is happy, only to their affliction, in the same way, perceptions and intentions accompanied by sensual desire occurred to me. That was an affliction for me.

“Then, Ānanda, the thought occurred to me: ‘What if, with the subsiding of thought (vitakka) and examination (vicāra)... I were to enter and dwell in the second jhāna?’ But my mind did not leap forward to the state without thought (avitakka), was not confident in it, did not become established in it, and was not released in it, seeing it as peaceful. Then, Ānanda, the thought occurred to me: ‘What is the cause, what is the reason, why my mind does not leap forward to the state without thought...?’ Then, Ānanda, the thought occurred to me: ‘I have not seen the danger in thoughts, nor have I cultivated that [vision]; I have not realized the benefit of the state without thought, nor have I pursued it. Therefore, my mind does not leap forward to the state without thought...’

“Then, Ānanda, the thought occurred to me: ‘If I were to see the danger in thoughts and cultivate that [vision], and if I were to realize the benefit of the state without thought and pursue it, then it is possible that my mind would leap forward to the state without thought, be confident in it, become established in it, and be released in it, seeing it as peaceful.’ Then, Ānanda, at a later time, having seen the danger in thoughts, I cultivated that [vision]; having realized the benefit of the state without thought, I pursued it. Then, Ānanda, my mind leaped forward to the state without thought, was confident in it, became established in it, and was released in it, seeing it as peaceful.

“Then, Ānanda, with the subsiding of thought and examination... I entered and dwelt in the second jhāna. While I was dwelling in this state, Ānanda, perceptions and intentions accompanied by thought occurred to me. That was an affliction for me. Ānanda, just as pain might arise for a person who is happy, only to their affliction, in the same way, perceptions and intentions accompanied by thought occurred to me. That was an affliction for me.

“Then, Ānanda, the thought occurred to me: ‘What if, with the fading away of rapture (pīti), I were to dwell equanimous, mindful and clearly comprehending, and experience happiness (sukha) with the body, entering and dwelling in the third jhāna, of which the Noble Ones declare: "He is equanimous, mindful, and dwells happily"?’ But my mind did not leap forward to the state without rapture...”
236:
'It would be good if I were to attain and dwell in the third jhāna.' Yet, Ānanda, my mind did not leap forward into that which is without rapture (the third jhāna), did not become clear, did not stand firm, and was not released into it, seeing it as peaceful. Then, Ānanda, the thought occurred to me: 'What is the cause, what is the reason why my mind does not leap forward, does not become clear, does not stand firm, and is not released into that which is without rapture, seeing it as peaceful?'

Then, Ānanda, the thought occurred to me: 'I have not seen the danger in rapture, nor have I cultivated that [vision]; I have not realized the benefit in that which is without rapture, nor have I pursued it. Therefore, my mind does not leap forward into that which is without rapture, does not become clear, does not stand firm, and is not released into it, seeing it as peaceful.'

Then, Ānanda, the thought occurred to me: 'If I were to see the danger in rapture and cultivate it, and if I were to realize the benefit in that which is without rapture and pursue it, it is possible that my mind would leap forward into that which is without rapture, become clear, stand firm, and be released into it, seeing it as peaceful.'

Then, Ānanda, at a later time, having seen the danger in rapture, I cultivated that [vision]; having realized the benefit in that which is without rapture, I pursued it. Then, Ānanda, my mind leaped forward into that which is without rapture, became clear, stood firm, and was released into it, seeing it as peaceful. Then, Ānanda, with the fading away of rapture... I attained and dwelt in the third jhāna. While I dwelt there, Ānanda, perceptions and attentions accompanied by rapture occurred. That was an affliction for me. Just as pain might arise for a happy person only to afflict him, so too perceptions and attentions accompanied by rapture occurred, and that was an affliction for me.

Then, Ānanda, the thought occurred to me: 'It would be good if, with the abandoning of pleasure and pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, I were to attain and dwell in the fourth jhāna, which has neither-pain-nor-pleasure and purity of mindfulness due to equanimity.' Yet, Ānanda, my mind did not leap forward into that which is neither-pain-nor-pleasure (the fourth jhāna), did not become clear, did not stand firm, and was not released into it, seeing it as peaceful. Then, Ānanda, the thought occurred to me: 'What is the cause, what is the reason why my mind does not leap forward into that which is neither-pain-nor-pleasure, does not become clear, does not stand firm, and is not released into it, seeing it as peaceful?'
237:
'...what is the support?'

Then, Ānanda, the thought occurred to me: 'I have not seen the danger in equanimity and pleasure (of the third jhāna), nor have I cultivated that [vision]; I have not realized the benefit in that which is neither-pain-nor-pleasure (the fourth jhāna), nor have I pursued it. Therefore, my mind does not leap forward into that which is neither-pain-nor-pleasure, does not become clear, does not stand firm, and is not released into it, seeing it as peaceful.'

Then, Ānanda, the thought occurred to me: 'If I were to see the danger in equanimity and pleasure and cultivate it, and if I were to realize the benefit in that which is neither-pain-nor-pleasure and pursue it, it is possible that my mind would leap forward into that which is neither-pain-nor-pleasure, become clear, stand firm, and be released into it, seeing it as peaceful.'

Then, Ānanda, at a later time, having seen the danger in equanimity and pleasure, I cultivated that [vision]; having realized the benefit in that which is neither-pain-nor-pleasure, I pursued it. Then, Ānanda, my mind leaped forward into that which is neither-pain-nor-pleasure, became clear, stood firm, and was released into it, seeing it as peaceful. Then, Ānanda, with the abandoning of pleasure... I attained and dwelt in the fourth jhāna. While I dwelt there, Ānanda, perceptions and attentions accompanied by equanimity occurred. That was an affliction for me. Just as pain might arise for a happy person only to afflict him, so too perceptions and attentions accompanied by equanimity occurred, and that was an affliction for me.

Then, Ānanda, the thought occurred to me: 'It would be good if, by completely transcending perceptions of form, with the disappearance of perceptions of sensory impact, and by not attending to perceptions of diversity, [perceiving] "space is infinite," I were to attain and dwell in the sphere of infinite space.' Yet, Ānanda, my mind did not leap forward into the sphere of infinite space, did not become clear, did not stand firm, and was not released into it, seeing it as peaceful. Then, Ānanda, the thought occurred to me: 'What is the cause, what is the reason why my mind does not leap forward into the sphere of infinite space, does not become clear, does not stand firm, and is not released into it, seeing it as peaceful? What is the support?'

Then, Ānanda, the thought occurred to me: 'I have not seen the danger in forms, nor have I cultivated that [vision]; I have not realized the benefit in the sphere of infinite space, nor have I pursued it. Therefore, my mind does not leap forward into the sphere of infinite space, does not become clear, does not stand firm, and is not released into it, seeing it as peaceful.'
238:
“Ānanda, it occurred to me: ‘If I were to see the danger in forms and cultivate that, and if I were to understand the benefit in the sphere of infinite space and pursue that, then it is possible that my mind—seeing it as peaceful—would leap forward into the sphere of infinite space, find confidence, settle, and be released.’ Ānanda, then at another time, having seen the danger in forms, I cultivated that; having understood the benefit in the sphere of infinite space, I pursued that. Ānanda, then my mind—seeing it as peaceful—leaped forward into the sphere of infinite space, found confidence, settled, and was released. Ānanda, with the complete surmounting of perceptions of form (rūpasaññā), with the passing away of perceptions of sensory impact (paṭighasaññā), with non-attention to perceptions of diversity (nānattasaññā), [perceiving] ‘space is infinite,’ I entered and dwelt in the sphere of infinite space (ākāsānañcāyatana).

Ānanda, while I dwelt in this state, perceptions and attentions accompanied by form occurred to me. That was an affliction for me. Just as, Ānanda, pain might arise for a happy person only to his affliction, so too, perceptions and attentions accompanied by form occurred to me. That was an affliction for me. Ānanda, it occurred to me: ‘What if, by completely surmounting the sphere of infinite space, [perceiving] “consciousness is infinite,” I were to enter and dwell in the sphere of infinite consciousness (viññāṇañcāyatana)?’ Ānanda, my mind—seeing it as peaceful—did not leap forward into the sphere of infinite consciousness, did not find confidence, did not settle, and was not released. Ānanda, it occurred to me: ‘What is the cause, what is the reason, why my mind—seeing it as peaceful—does not leap forward into the sphere of infinite consciousness, find confidence, settle, and become released?’ Ānanda, it occurred to me: ‘I have not seen the danger in the sphere of infinite space, and I have not cultivated that; I have not realized the benefit in the sphere of infinite consciousness, and I have not pursued that. Therefore, my mind—seeing it as peaceful—does not leap forward into the sphere of infinite consciousness, find confidence, settle, and become released.’ Ānanda, it occurred to me: ‘If I were to see the danger in the sphere of infinite space and cultivate that, and if I were to understand the benefit in the sphere of infinite consciousness and pursue that, then it is possible that my mind—seeing it as peaceful—would leap forward into the sphere of infinite consciousness, find confidence, settle, and be released.’ Ānanda, then at another time, having seen the danger in the sphere of infinite space, I cultivated that;”
239:
“I understood the benefit in the sphere of infinite consciousness and pursued that. Ānanda, then my mind—seeing it as peaceful—leaped forward into the sphere of infinite consciousness, found confidence, settled, and was released. Ānanda, by completely surmounting the sphere of infinite space, [perceiving] ‘consciousness is infinite,’ I entered and dwelt in the sphere of infinite consciousness (viññāṇañcāyatana). Ānanda, while I dwelt in this state, perceptions and attentions accompanied by the sphere of infinite space occurred to me. That was an affliction for me. Ānanda, just as pain might arise for a happy person only to his affliction, so too, perceptions and attentions accompanied by the sphere of infinite space occurred to me. That was an affliction for me. Ānanda, it occurred to me: ‘What if, by completely surmounting the sphere of infinite consciousness, [perceiving] “there is nothing,” I were to enter and dwell in the sphere of nothingness (ākiñcaññāyatana)?’ Ānanda, my mind—seeing it as peaceful—did not leap forward into the sphere of nothingness, did not find confidence, did not settle, and was not released. Ānanda, it occurred to me: ‘What is the cause, what is the reason, why my mind—seeing it as peaceful—does not leap forward into the sphere of nothingness, find confidence, settle, and become released?’ Ānanda, it occurred to me: ‘I have not seen the danger in the sphere of infinite consciousness, and I have not cultivated that; I have not realized the benefit in the sphere of nothingness, and I have not pursued that. Therefore, my mind—seeing it as peaceful—does not leap forward into the sphere of nothingness, find confidence, settle, and become released.’ Ānanda, it occurred to me: ‘If I were to see the danger in the sphere of infinite consciousness and cultivate that, and if I were to understand the benefit in the sphere of nothingness and pursue that, then it is possible that my mind—seeing it as peaceful—would leap forward into the sphere of infinite consciousness [Note: likely should be sphere of nothingness based on context] find confidence, settle, and be released.’

Ānanda, then at another time, having seen the danger in the sphere of infinite consciousness, I cultivated that; having understood the benefit in the sphere of nothingness, I pursued that. Ānanda, then my mind—seeing it as peaceful—leaped forward into the sphere of nothingness, found confidence, settled, and was released. Ānanda, by completely surmounting the sphere of infinite consciousness, [perceiving] ‘there is nothing,’ I entered and dwelt in the sphere of nothingness. Ānanda, while I dwelt in this state, perceptions and attentions accompanied by the sphere of infinite consciousness occurred to me. That was an affliction for me. Ānanda, just as pain might arise for a happy person only to his affliction,”
240:
In the same way, perceptions and intentions accompanied by the sphere of infinite consciousness occurred to me, and that occurrence was an affliction for me. Ānanda, the thought occurred to me: 'It would be good if, having completely transcended the sphere of nothingness, I were to enter and dwell in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.' Yet, Ānanda, my mind did not leap forward into the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, nor did it take satisfaction in it, nor stand firm in it, nor release into it, seeing it as peaceful.

Ānanda, the thought occurred to me: 'What is the cause, what is the reason, why my mind does not leap forward into the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, nor take satisfaction in it, nor stand firm in it, nor release into it, seeing it as peaceful?' Ānanda, the thought occurred to me: 'I have not seen the danger in the sphere of nothingness, nor have I cultivated that [insight]; and I have not realized the benefit in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, nor have I pursued it. Therefore, my mind does not leap forward into the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, nor take satisfaction in it, nor stand firm in it, nor release into it, seeing it as peaceful.'

Ānanda, the thought occurred to me: 'If I were to see the danger in the sphere of nothingness and cultivate that [insight], and if I were to realize the benefit in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception and pursue it, then it is possible that my mind would leap forward into the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, take satisfaction in it, stand firm in it, and be released into it, seeing it as peaceful.'

Ānanda, at a later time, having seen the danger in the sphere of nothingness, I cultivated that [insight]; and having realized the benefit in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, I pursued it. Then, Ānanda, my mind leaped forward into the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, took satisfaction in it, stood firm in it, and was released into it, seeing it as peaceful. Ānanda, having completely transcended the sphere of nothingness, I entered and dwelt in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

Ānanda, while I was dwelling in this attainment, perceptions and intentions accompanied by the sphere of nothingness occurred to me, and that occurrence was an affliction for me. Just as, Ānanda, pain might arise for a happy person only to his affliction, in the same way, perceptions and intentions accompanied by the sphere of nothingness occurred to me, and that occurrence was an affliction for me.

Ānanda, the thought occurred to me: 'It would be good if, having completely transcended the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, I were to enter and dwell in the cessation of perception and feeling.' Yet, Ānanda, my mind did not leap forward into the cessation of perception and feeling, nor take satisfaction in it, nor stand firm in it, nor release into it, seeing it as peaceful. Ānanda, the thought occurred to me: 'What is the cause, what is the reason, why my mind does not leap forward into the cessation of perception and feeling, nor take satisfaction in it, nor stand firm in it, nor release into it, seeing it as peaceful?'
241:
The thought occurred to me: 'What is the support?' Ānanda, it occurred to me: 'I have not seen the danger in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, nor have I pursued that danger. I have not realized the benefit in the cessation of perception and feeling (nirodha-samāpatti), nor have I cultivated that benefit. Therefore, my mind does not leap forward into the cessation of perception and feeling, nor does it acquire confidence, settle, or resolve upon it, even though I see it as peaceful.'

Ānanda, it occurred to me: 'If I were to see the danger in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception and pursue it, and if I were to realize the benefit in the cessation of perception and feeling and cultivate it, then it is possible that my mind would leap forward into the cessation of perception and feeling, acquire confidence, settle, and resolve upon it, seeing it as peaceful.' Ānanda, at a later time, having seen the danger in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, I pursued it; having realized the benefit in the cessation of perception and feeling, I cultivated it. Ānanda, my mind leaped forward into the cessation of perception and feeling, acquired confidence, settled, and resolved upon it, seeing it as peaceful. Ānanda, by completely transcending the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, I entered and dwelt in the cessation of perception and feeling. As long, Ānanda, as I did not attain and emerge from these nine successive dwellings (samāpatti) in both forward and reverse order, I did not claim to have awakened to the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment (anuttaraṃ sammāsambodhiṃ) in this world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, in this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its princes and humans. ## 10. Cetaso Vinibandha Sutta

92. Monks, there are these five mental fetters (cetaso vinibandhā). What five? Here, monks, a monk is not free from lust for sensual pleasures... [pe]... Monks, these are the five mental fetters. Monks, for the abandoning of these five mental fetters, these four bases of power should be developed. What four? Here, monks, a monk develops the base of power that possesses concentration due to desire and volitional formations of striving. He develops the base of power that possesses concentration due to energy... concentration due to mind... concentration due to investigation and volitional formations of striving. Monks, for the abandoning of these five mental fetters, these four bases of power should be developed.
